posts.title: Why Did Humans Even Invent Computers?

slides.headline: Four hours re-doing a payroll sheet by hand, and I still shipped two wrong cells
slides.text: One broken formula meant redoing thousands of tiny sums manually — and human arithmetic doesn't stay correct at volume.

slides.headline: The bottleneck was never the math. It was us.
slides.text: Each operation was trivial. Doing thousands of them exactly, without fatigue or a slipped digit, is precisely where humans fail.

slides.headline: So we built a machine to do the exact, boring part
slides.text: A computer follows fixed rules over huge amounts of data and returns the same answer every single time — no tiredness, no drift.

slides.headline: Humans bring judgment. Machines bring tireless precision.
slides.text: We kept deciding what to compute; the machine took over doing it — fast, identical, at any scale. That division of labour is the whole point.

slides.headline: Computers exist because humans are slow and error-prone at exact, repetitive work — and machines aren't
slides.text: That one trade-off is the seed of every track that follows.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: The Minds Before Computers Existed

posts.title: The Minds Before Computers Existed

slides.headline: People designed a general-purpose computer a full century before one could be built
slides.text: Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for a machine that didn't physically exist yet.

slides.headline: The hard part was never the wires — it was the idea
slides.text: Before hardware, someone had to imagine a single machine that could follow any set of instructions, not just one fixed task.

slides.headline: Babbage designed it, Lovelace programmed it, Turing proved it
slides.text: Babbage's Analytical Engine had a processor and memory on paper; Lovelace saw it could manipulate symbols, not just numbers; Turing defined what such a machine could and couldn't compute.

slides.headline: A special-purpose machine does one job; a general-purpose one does any job you can describe
slides.text: The leap was from 'a device that adds' to 'a device that runs whatever instructions you feed it.'

slides.headline: The computer was invented as an idea long before it was invented as a machine
slides.text: Hardware caught up to a concept that was already complete.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: From Mainframes to AI Computers: The Full Evolution

posts.title: From Mainframes to AI Computers: The Full Evolution

slides.headline: The same computing idea has fit in a room, a desk, a pocket, and now a data-centre rack
slides.text: Nothing about the core idea changed — only its cost and size.

slides.headline: Each era solved 'who can afford a computer?' one step further
slides.text: Mainframes served whole companies, PCs served individuals, the cloud rents computing by the second, and AI chips specialise it.

slides.headline: Mainframe to PC to cloud to AI accelerator
slides.text: Shrinking transistors made machines cheaper and smaller; the network let us rent them remotely; AI workloads pushed us back toward specialised hardware built for one kind of math.

slides.headline: General-purpose CPUs do anything adequately; AI accelerators do one thing spectacularly
slides.text: We spent decades generalising the computer, then started specialising it again for machine learning.

slides.headline: The computer never got a new idea — it just got cheaper, smaller, and rentable
slides.text: Every revolution in this story is the same machine, more accessible.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is a Computer, Really?

posts.title: What Is a Computer, Really?

slides.headline: Strip away the screen, the OS, the apps — what's actually left?
slides.text: Underneath everything, a computer is doing four things in a loop.

slides.headline: A computer is a machine that follows instructions over data
slides.text: It takes input, processes it by rule, stores intermediate results, and produces output. That's the entire job description.

slides.headline: Input, process, store, output — on repeat, billions of times a second
slides.text: Data comes in, the processor transforms it step by step using stored instructions, and results go out. Everything else is a layer on top of this cycle.

slides.headline: Instructions and data are both just numbers in memory — the CPU tells them apart by role
slides.text: A byte isn't 'code' or 'data' by nature; it's whichever the processor treats it as right now.

slides.headline: A computer is an instruction-follower, not a thinker — it does exactly what it's told, very fast
slides.text: Its power is obedience at scale, not intelligence.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Von Neumann vs Harvard: Two Ways to Build a Computer

posts.title: Von Neumann vs Harvard: Two Ways to Build a Computer

slides.headline: Two computers can be built on opposite wiring choices and you'd never know from the outside
slides.text: The difference is where instructions and data live.

slides.headline: The question: should code and data share one memory, or get separate ones?
slides.text: Every processor answers this, and the answer shapes speed, flexibility, and safety.

slides.headline: Von Neumann shares one memory bus; Harvard splits instructions and data apart
slides.text: One shared path is simpler and lets programs modify themselves; two separate paths let the CPU fetch an instruction and its data at the same time.

slides.headline: Shared memory: flexible but bottlenecked. Split memory: fast but rigid.
slides.text: Von Neumann's single bus is a traffic jam under load; Harvard's dual bus is faster but harder to reprogram — which is why microcontrollers often use it and general computers don't.

slides.headline: Von Neumann trades speed for flexibility; Harvard trades flexibility for speed
slides.text: The wiring choice is a bet on what the machine will be used for.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: x86 vs ARM: Instruction Set Architectures & Pipelining

posts.title: x86 vs ARM: Instruction Set Architectures & Pipelining

slides.headline: The same app runs on your laptop and your phone, but the chips speak different languages
slides.text: x86 and ARM don't share an instruction set.

slides.headline: An instruction set is the vocabulary a CPU understands
slides.text: x86 offers many complex instructions (CISC); ARM offers fewer, simpler ones (RISC) that the chip runs faster and with less power.

slides.headline: Pipelining lets a CPU work on several instructions at once
slides.text: Like an assembly line, one instruction is decoded while the next is fetched and the previous one executes — simpler instructions keep that line flowing smoothly.

slides.headline: x86: raw performance, more power draw. ARM: efficiency, longer battery.
slides.text: Complex instructions do more per step but stall the pipeline; simple instructions do less per step but keep it full — which is why phones favour ARM and desktops long favoured x86.

slides.headline: CISC packs power into each instruction; RISC packs speed into simple ones done relentlessly
slides.text: Neither is 'better' — they optimise for different constraints.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Bits, Bytes & Binary: The Language of Machines

posts.title: Bits, Bytes & Binary: The Language of Machines

slides.headline: Every photo, song, and message on your machine is really just two symbols: on and off
slides.text: There is nothing else underneath.

slides.headline: A bit is one on/off switch; a byte is eight of them
slides.text: Eight bits give 256 combinations — enough to encode a letter, a small number, or a shade of colour.

slides.headline: Meaning comes from agreed encodings, not from the bits themselves
slides.text: 01000001 is the letter 'A' only because ASCII says so. Change the encoding and the same bits become a number or a pixel.

slides.headline: Binary is fragile in meaning but rock-solid in hardware
slides.text: Two clean voltage levels are trivial for a circuit to tell apart, which is why everything is built on base-2 instead of base-10.

slides.headline: Computers don't store letters or colours — they store switches, and we agree what the switches mean
slides.text: All data is interpretation layered on on/off.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Logic Gates: How Computers Think

posts.title: Logic Gates: How Computers Think

slides.headline: How does a box of switches ever 'decide' anything?
slides.text: With three tiny operations, and nothing more.

slides.headline: Logic gates turn on/off inputs into on/off outputs by rule
slides.text: AND outputs on only if both inputs are on; OR if either is; NOT flips its input. That's the entire toolkit.

slides.headline: Combine gates and you can build addition, comparison, memory
slides.text: Wire enough AND/OR/NOT together and you get an adder; loop them back and you get a circuit that remembers a bit.

slides.headline: A single gate is trivial; millions of them wired together is a processor
slides.text: Complexity here isn't clever parts — it's simple parts repeated at enormous scale.

slides.headline: Every 'decision' a computer makes reduces to AND, OR, and NOT on switches
slides.text: Intelligence is not in the gate — it's in the arrangement.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Transistors to CPU: The Brain of the Machine

posts.title: Transistors to CPU: The Brain of the Machine

slides.headline: A modern CPU has billions of transistors, and each one only does one thing
slides.text: A transistor is a switch that electricity controls — no moving parts, just on or off.

slides.headline: A transistor is an electrically-controlled on/off switch
slides.text: Feed it a signal and it opens or closes a circuit. Group a few and you've built a logic gate.

slides.headline: Transistors to gates to ALU to CPU
slides.text: Gates form arithmetic units; arithmetic units plus registers and a control unit form a processor that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions.

slides.headline: Smaller transistors mean more of them, but heat becomes the wall
slides.text: Shrinking lets us pack more computing into a chip — until the density traps so much heat that speed gains stall. That's why clock speeds plateaued.

slides.headline: A CPU is billions of the same tiny switch, arranged to fetch, decode, and execute
slides.text: The brain of the machine is repetition, not magic.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Cache, RAM & Storage: Where Computers Keep Memories

posts.title: Cache, RAM & Storage: Where Computers Keep Memories

slides.headline: Why does your machine have RAM and storage instead of just one big memory?
slides.text: Because no single memory is both fast and cheap.

slides.headline: Memory forms a hierarchy: cache, RAM, disk
slides.text: Cache is tiny and blazing fast, RAM is larger and fast, storage is huge and slow but keeps data when the power is off.

slides.headline: The CPU checks the fastest memory first, falling back as it misses
slides.text: Wanted data in cache? Instant. Not there? Check RAM. Not there? Load from disk — orders of magnitude slower each step down.

slides.headline: Speed, capacity, and cost pull against each other
slides.text: Fast memory is expensive and small; cheap memory is slow and large. The hierarchy is how we get the feel of fast-and-huge without paying for it.

slides.headline: The memory hierarchy is a bet: keep what you'll need soon close, and everything else far but cheap
slides.text: Fast, big, cheap — pick two, then layer them.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: GPU, Motherboard & I/O: Completing the Machine

posts.title: GPU, Motherboard & I/O: Completing the Machine

slides.headline: The CPU gets all the credit, but it can't draw a pixel or save a file alone
slides.text: It needs the rest of the machine.

slides.headline: GPU, motherboard, and I/O complete the computer
slides.text: The GPU does massively parallel work like graphics; the motherboard's buses connect everything; I/O moves data between the machine and the outside world.

slides.headline: A CPU does a few things fast in sequence; a GPU does thousands of things at once
slides.text: For one hard calculation, the CPU wins. For the same simple calculation on a million pixels, the GPU's parallel cores win — which is also why they run AI math.

slides.headline: Buses trade simplicity for shared bandwidth
slides.text: One shared pathway keeps the design simple but forces components to take turns; dedicated lanes are faster but cost more wiring and pins.

slides.headline: The CPU thinks in sequence, the GPU thinks in parallel, and buses let them all talk
slides.text: A computer is a team of specialised parts, not one hero chip.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: From Machine Code to Real Programming Languages

posts.title: From Machine Code to Real Programming Languages

slides.headline: Nobody writes real software in ones and zeros — so how did we escape machine code?
slides.text: By stacking layers of translation.

slides.headline: Programming languages are abstractions over machine code
slides.text: Machine code is raw numbers the CPU runs; assembly names those numbers; high-level languages let you write intent that gets translated down to them.

slides.headline: Each layer trades control for readability
slides.text: Assembly maps almost one-to-one to CPU instructions; a language like Python hides registers and memory entirely so you can think in problems, not hardware.

slides.headline: Low-level: total control, painful to write. High-level: fast to write, less control.
slides.text: You give up knowing exactly what the CPU does in exchange for expressing ideas in far less code — usually a good trade, occasionally not.

slides.headline: A programming language is a human-readable disguise over machine code
slides.text: We didn't make the CPU smarter — we made the instructions easier to write.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Compilers vs Interpreters: What Actually Runs Your Code

posts.title: Compilers vs Interpreters: What Actually Runs Your Code

slides.headline: Your source code can't run — the CPU has never seen a for-loop in its life
slides.text: Something has to translate it first.

slides.headline: Compilers and interpreters both bridge source code to machine code — differently
slides.text: A compiler translates the whole program ahead of time into an executable; an interpreter translates and runs it line by line as it goes.

slides.headline: Compile once and run fast, or skip the wait and run as you go
slides.text: Compiled code starts slower to build but runs fast and ships as a standalone binary; interpreted code runs immediately but re-translates every time it executes.

slides.headline: Compilers trade startup time for run speed; interpreters trade run speed for flexibility
slides.text: C compiles to fast native binaries but must be rebuilt; Python runs instantly and portably but pays a speed cost each execution.

slides.headline: Compile now to run fast later, or interpret now to run flexibly today
slides.text: Same goal, opposite timing of the translation.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Really Happens Inside Your Computer When You Run a Program

posts.title: What Really Happens Inside Your Computer When You Run a Program

slides.headline: You double-click an app. Between that click and the window opening, a lot happens.
slides.text: Here's the actual sequence.

slides.headline: Running a program means loading its instructions into memory and pointing the CPU at them
slides.text: The file on disk is inert; execution is the OS copying it into RAM and handing control to the CPU.

slides.headline: Source, translate, load, execute
slides.text: Code is compiled or interpreted into machine instructions, the OS loads the program into memory as a process, and the CPU fetches and runs those instructions one by one.

slides.headline: On disk a program is data; in memory it's a running process
slides.text: The same bytes are passive storage until the OS gives them a slice of memory, CPU time, and the right to act.

slides.headline: A program is just a file until the OS loads it into memory and lets the CPU run it
slides.text: Execution is a file being given life by the operating system.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Does Every Computer Need an Operating System?

posts.title: Why Does Every Computer Need an Operating System?

slides.headline: Your laptop runs a browser, music, and twenty background tasks — none of them fighting over the CPU
slides.text: Something is refereeing all of it.

slides.headline: An operating system manages the hardware so programs don't have to
slides.text: It decides which program gets the CPU, how memory is shared, and how apps reach the disk, network, and screen without colliding.

slides.headline: The OS sits between your apps and the bare metal
slides.text: Apps ask the OS for resources through system calls; the OS grants, schedules, and protects — so no single app can seize the whole machine or read another's memory.

slides.headline: Without an OS, one program owns everything; with one, everything shares safely
slides.text: Direct hardware access is faster but chaotic; a managed layer costs a little overhead to buy multitasking, isolation, and security.

slides.headline: The OS is the referee that lets many programs share one machine without stepping on each other
slides.text: Its job is arbitration, not computation.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Processes, Threads & the Art of Multitasking

posts.title: Processes, Threads & the Art of Multitasking

slides.headline: Your CPU has a handful of cores, yet hundreds of tasks 'run at once' — how?
slides.text: By switching faster than you can notice.

slides.headline: A process is a running program; a thread is a task inside it
slides.text: Each process gets its own isolated memory; threads inside a process share that memory to work together on one job.

slides.headline: The scheduler slices CPU time and switches between tasks constantly
slides.text: Each task runs for a few milliseconds, then the OS saves its state and swaps in another — fast enough that everything feels simultaneous.

slides.headline: Threads share memory cheaply but can corrupt it; processes are isolated but costlier to coordinate
slides.text: Sharing memory makes threads fast to communicate and dangerous to get wrong; separate memory makes processes safe but slower to talk between.

slides.headline: Multitasking is illusion by speed — one core, many tasks, switched too fast to see
slides.text: Concurrency is mostly clever scheduling, not literal simultaneity.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Memory Management: How the OS Juggles Everything

posts.title: Memory Management: How the OS Juggles Everything

slides.headline: You've opened more tabs than you have RAM, and nothing crashed — where did the extra memory come from?
slides.text: It was never entirely real.

slides.headline: The OS gives every process its own private, virtual view of memory
slides.text: Each program thinks it owns a clean address space; the OS secretly maps those virtual addresses onto real RAM and disk.

slides.headline: Virtual memory and paging stretch RAM further than it physically goes
slides.text: Memory is split into pages; rarely-used pages get parked on disk and swapped back in on demand, so more can 'fit' than physically exists.

slides.headline: Virtual memory buys isolation and capacity, at the cost of speed when it swaps
slides.text: Every process is protected from every other, and you can run more than fits — until heavy swapping to disk grinds things to a crawl (thrashing).

slides.headline: Virtual memory is a lie the OS tells every program: 'the RAM is all yours'
slides.text: The illusion is what keeps programs isolated and safe.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: System Calls, Drivers & the Big 3 Operating Systems

posts.title: System Calls, Drivers & the Big 3 Operating Systems

slides.headline: Your code wants to read a file, but it's not allowed to touch the disk directly
slides.text: It has to ask the kernel.

slides.headline: A system call is how a program requests a privileged operation from the OS
slides.text: Reading files, opening sockets, spawning processes — all cross the boundary from user space into the protected kernel.

slides.headline: Drivers translate generic OS requests into device-specific commands
slides.text: Your app says 'write these bytes'; the OS routes it through a driver that knows how to speak to that exact disk, GPU, or network card.

slides.headline: Windows, macOS, and Linux differ on top but all guard the kernel boundary
slides.text: They expose different APIs and philosophies, yet each separates untrusted user code from privileged hardware access the same way.

slides.headline: A system call is the guarded door between your program and the hardware it isn't allowed to touch
slides.text: User space asks; the kernel decides.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Actually Happens When You Open Chrome or Run a Terminal Command

posts.title: What Actually Happens When You Open Chrome or Run a Terminal Command

slides.headline: You type a command or click an icon, and a new program springs into existence
slides.text: What actually creates it?

slides.headline: Launching a program means the OS creates a new process for it
slides.text: It allocates memory, loads the executable, sets up its environment, and schedules it to run.

slides.headline: On Unix, one process clones itself, then becomes the new program
slides.text: fork() copies the current process; exec() replaces that copy's code with the program you asked for — that pair is how the shell runs everything you type.

slides.headline: Fork-then-exec is elegant but copies state; spawning fresh avoids the copy but loses inheritance
slides.text: Cloning lets a child inherit the parent's setup cheaply; a from-scratch spawn is cleaner but has to rebuild context.

slides.headline: Opening an app is the OS cloning a process and swapping in your program's code
slides.text: Every launch is birth by fork and exec.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is Programming, Actually?

posts.title: What Is Programming, Actually?

slides.headline: 'Just tell the computer what to do' — except it does exactly what you say, not what you mean
slides.text: That gap is the whole craft.

slides.headline: Programming is expressing a solution as instructions precise enough for a machine
slides.text: The hard part isn't syntax — it's turning a fuzzy human goal into unambiguous, ordered steps.

slides.headline: You break a problem into steps, encode them, and the machine executes literally
slides.text: No step can be assumed. The computer has no common sense to fill gaps, so every case must be spelled out.

slides.headline: Humans tolerate ambiguity; computers punish it
slides.text: A recipe that says 'season to taste' works for a cook and fails for a machine — programming is removing every 'to taste.'

slides.headline: Programming is the art of being so precise that a machine can't misunderstand you
slides.text: It's specifying, not suggesting.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Imperative vs Declarative: Two Ways to Tell a Computer What to Do

posts.title: Imperative vs Declarative: Two Ways to Tell a Computer What to Do

slides.headline: Two programs solve the same task — one lists every step, the other just describes the result
slides.text: Both are valid. They're opposite styles.

slides.headline: Imperative code says how; declarative code says what
slides.text: Imperative spells out each step to reach the answer; declarative states the goal and lets the system figure out the steps.

slides.headline: A loop that filters a list vs a query that describes the filter
slides.text: Writing 'for each item, if it matches, keep it' is imperative; writing 'give me items where x is true' (like SQL) is declarative.

slides.headline: Imperative gives control; declarative gives brevity
slides.text: Step-by-step code lets you tune exactly how work happens; describing the outcome is shorter and clearer but hides — and limits — your control over the how.

slides.headline: Imperative tells the computer the steps; declarative tells it the destination
slides.text: Choose control or clarity depending on which the problem needs.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: The Building Blocks Every Programmer Learns First

posts.title: The Building Blocks Every Programmer Learns First

slides.headline: Almost every program you'll ever write is built from the same four ideas
slides.text: Master these and the rest is variation.

slides.headline: Variables, conditionals, loops, and functions are the core
slides.text: Variables hold state, conditionals choose paths, loops repeat work, and functions package logic to reuse.

slides.headline: Combine the four and you can express any computation
slides.text: Store a value, branch on it, repeat over a collection, and factor the repeated part into a function — that's the shape of nearly all code.

slides.headline: More abstraction (functions) reduces repetition but adds indirection
slides.text: Pulling logic into functions keeps code DRY and readable; overdo it and a reader has to jump around to follow a simple flow.

slides.headline: Variables, conditionals, loops, functions — every program is a remix of these four
slides.text: Learn the primitives and languages become dialects.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Functional Programming: Pure Functions & Immutability

posts.title: Functional Programming: Pure Functions & Immutability

slides.headline: A function that changes nothing but its return value is weirdly easy to trust
slides.text: That's the whole pitch of functional programming.

slides.headline: Pure functions and immutability are the core of the functional style
slides.text: A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself; immutable data is never modified in place, only copied.

slides.headline: No hidden state means no surprise bugs from shared data
slides.text: Because a pure function can't secretly alter something elsewhere, you can test it in isolation and reason about it without tracking the rest of the program.

slides.headline: Purity buys predictability; it costs some performance and convenience
slides.text: Copying data instead of mutating it is safer and easier to parallelise, but creates more objects and can feel verbose for simple in-place updates.

slides.headline: A pure function is a promise: same input in, same output out, nothing touched on the side
slides.text: Predictability is the feature you're buying.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Scope, Recursion & Handling Errors Like a Pro

posts.title: Scope, Recursion & Handling Errors Like a Pro

slides.headline: A variable that worked everywhere suddenly 'doesn't exist' — welcome to scope
slides.text: Where a name lives decides where it works.

slides.headline: Scope defines where a name is visible; recursion is a function calling itself
slides.text: Variables declared inside a function usually can't be seen outside it; a recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece.

slides.headline: Recursion needs a base case, or it never stops
slides.text: Each call must shrink the problem and there must be a case that returns without recursing — miss it and the call stack overflows.

slides.headline: Recursion is elegant for nested problems but heavier than a loop
slides.text: It reads cleanly for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call uses stack memory a loop wouldn't — deep recursion can crash where a loop wouldn't.

slides.headline: Scope decides where a name lives; recursion works only if it knows when to stop
slides.text: Both are about boundaries — of visibility and of repetition.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Modules, Libraries, Packages & APIs Explained

posts.title: Modules, Libraries, Packages & APIs Explained

slides.headline: You'll write far less code than you import — most software is other people's code
slides.text: Reuse is the norm, not the exception.

slides.headline: Modules, libraries, packages, and APIs are all about reusing code
slides.text: A module is a file of related code; a library is a bundle you call; a package is a shippable library; an API is the agreed way to call code you don't own.

slides.headline: You import a package, call its functions through its API, and skip reinventing it
slides.text: Instead of writing date-parsing or HTTP handling yourself, you pull in a tested package and use its documented interface.

slides.headline: Dependencies save time but become risk you don't control
slides.text: Reusing a library is faster and better-tested than DIY, but every dependency adds surface area for bugs, breaking changes, and security holes.

slides.headline: An API is a contract: use this code without knowing how it works inside
slides.text: Reuse is leverage — and a debt you take on.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is an Algorithm? (And Why Coding Is Not Problem Solving)

posts.title: What Is an Algorithm? (And Why Coding Is Not Problem Solving)

slides.headline: You can know every language feature and still not be able to solve the problem
slides.text: Coding and problem-solving are different skills.

slides.headline: An algorithm is a precise, finite procedure that solves a class of problems
slides.text: It's the strategy — the sequence of steps that turns any valid input into the correct output — independent of the language you write it in.

slides.headline: Understand the problem, design the steps, then translate to code
slides.text: The thinking happens before the typing: what are the inputs, the constraints, the approach? Code is just the last step.

slides.headline: Syntax is learnable in weeks; algorithmic thinking takes real practice
slides.text: Knowing how to write a loop is easy; knowing which loop, over what structure, in what order, is the skill that transfers across every language.

slides.headline: Coding is how you tell the computer; the algorithm is what you decided to tell it
slides.text: The problem is solved before a single line is written.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Big O Notation: The Skill That Separates Junior From Senior

posts.title: Big O Notation: The Skill That Separates Junior From Senior

slides.headline: Your code ran fine in the demo and timed out on real data — the difference is Big O
slides.text: It's the skill that separates junior from senior.

slides.headline: Big O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as input grows
slides.text: It ignores seconds and hardware and asks the only question that scales: when the input gets 10x bigger, does the work get 10x, 100x, or barely bigger?

slides.headline: O(1), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) — the shape matters more than the constant
slides.text: A nested loop is O(n²): fine at 100 items, catastrophic at a million. A single pass is O(n). A good sort is O(n log n).

slides.headline: A slower Big O beats a faster machine at scale, every time
slides.text: Throwing hardware at an O(n²) algorithm buys a little room; changing it to O(n log n) buys orders of magnitude — that's why the curve, not the constant, decides.

slides.headline: Big O isn't about how fast it runs — it's about how badly it breaks when the input grows
slides.text: Optimise the growth curve before the constant.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Arrays, Strings & Linked Lists: Where Everyone Starts

posts.title: Arrays, Strings & Linked Lists: Where Everyone Starts

slides.headline: Arrays
slides.text: Think of a movie theater: seat 47 is seat 47, no scanning seats 1-46 to find it. That's an array — a fixed-size, ordered block of memory where every item sits at a numbered position, so reading any item is instant (O(1)), no matter the size.

slides.headline: Strings
slides.text: A string is just an array of characters treated as text — same rules apply: fast to read by position, but its size is locked in from the moment it's created.

slides.headline: Linked Lists
slides.text: Like a treasure hunt where each clue only reveals the next one: a linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next. Inserting is just two pointer updates — instant, even in a list of 10 million. The tradeoff: to find anything, you start at the beginning and follow the chain, one step at a time.

slides.text: you'll run into arrays, strings & linked lists: where everyone starts on your first real project — probably before you feel ready for it.

posts.title: Stacks, Queues & Hash Tables Explained

slides.headline: Stack
slides.text: Picture a stack of plates — you only ever add or remove from the top, never the middle or bottom. That's Last-In-First-Out. It's why Ctrl+Z works, why your browser's back button peels off the most recent page first, and how the call stack tracks which function returns next.

slides.headline: Queue
slides.text: A queue is a line at a coffee shop — first person in line, first one served, no cutting. Enqueue adds to the back, dequeue removes from the front. It's how print jobs line up and how web servers process thousands of incoming requests in order.

slides.headline: Hash Tables
slides.text: Search 'mom' in your contacts and her number appears instantly — that's a hash table. A hash function turns the key into a number that points straight to a memory slot, so lookup is O(1) whether you have 10 contacts or 10 million. The cost: more memory, and occasional collisions when two keys land on the same slot.

posts.title: Trees, Heaps & Graphs: Where DSA Gets Real

slides.headline: Trees
slides.text: Open your file explorer: one root at the top, branching into folders, then files — every path flows one direction, root to leaves, with no cycles. That's a tree. HTML's DOM, comment threads, and decision trees all follow the same branching shape.

slides.headline: Heaps
slides.text: Like an ER: the heart attack patient gets seen before the headache, no matter who arrived first. A heap keeps the highest-priority item at the top at all times, reorganizing itself on every insert or removal — which is exactly how OS task schedulers and GPS route recalculation work.

slides.headline: Graphs
slides.text: Facebook is one giant graph — you're a node, friendships are edges. Google Maps is another — cities are nodes, roads are edges, and 'get directions' is just a search across it. Graphs can be directed (Twitter follows) or undirected (Facebook friends), stored as an adjacency matrix (fast lookups) or adjacency list (more memory-efficient), and explored with DFS or BFS.

posts.title: Searching & Sorting: The Algorithms Behind Everything

slides.headline: 'Find this item' and 'put these in order' are behind a shocking amount of software
slides.text: Searching and sorting are everywhere.

slides.headline: Searching finds an item; sorting arranges items so searching gets cheaper
slides.text: Sorted data unlocks fast lookups; much of the value of sorting is making later searches efficient.

slides.headline: Binary search halves the problem each step — but only on sorted data
slides.text: Linear search checks every item; binary search jumps to the middle and discards half each time, turning a million-item search into about twenty steps.

slides.headline: Faster search needs sorted data, and good sorting costs O(n log n)
slides.text: You pay the sort once to make every future search O(log n) — worth it when you search often, wasteful when you search once.

slides.headline: Sort once to search fast forever — the two algorithms pay for each other
slides.text: Order is an investment that searching cashes in.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Recursion, Backtracking, Greedy & DP: The Hard Stuff

posts.title: Recursion, Backtracking, Greedy & DP: The Hard Stuff

slides.headline: Some problems have too many possibilities to brute-force and too much overlap to ignore
slides.text: This is where the hard techniques earn their keep.

slides.headline: Recursion, backtracking, greedy, and dynamic programming are problem-solving strategies
slides.text: Recursion breaks a problem into smaller copies; backtracking tries paths and undoes dead ends; greedy takes the best local step; DP caches overlapping subproblems.

slides.headline: DP turns exponential recursion into something practical by remembering answers
slides.text: A naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values millions of times; storing each result once collapses it from exponential to linear.

slides.headline: Greedy is fast but can be wrong; DP is correct but costs memory
slides.text: A greedy choice is quick and sometimes optimal; dynamic programming guarantees the best answer but stores every subproblem — time for space.

slides.headline: Backtracking explores, greedy gambles, DP remembers — the hard problems need the right strategy, not more speed
slides.text: Technique beats brute force where the search space explodes.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Software Engineering vs Just Writing Code

posts.title: Software Engineering vs Just Writing Code

slides.headline: The code was fine. The project still failed — late, unmaintainable, and impossible to hand off.
slides.text: Writing code and engineering software aren't the same job.

slides.headline: Software engineering is building software that survives people, time, and change
slides.text: It adds the things a working script lacks: tests, version control, documentation, review, and a design that others can extend.

slides.headline: Engineering optimises for the second reader and the sixth month
slides.text: Code is written once and read many times; the discipline is making it correct, understandable, and changeable long after you've forgotten it.

slides.headline: A clever script solves today; engineered software keeps solving as requirements shift
slides.text: Raw coding wins a hackathon; engineering wins the five years of maintenance nobody demos.

slides.headline: Writing code makes it work once; software engineering makes it keep working as everything changes
slides.text: The hard part is not the first version — it's the fiftieth.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: The Software Lifecycle: Build, Test, Ship, Maintain

posts.title: The Software Lifecycle: Build, Test, Ship, Maintain

slides.headline: Shipping isn't the finish line — most of a product's life happens after launch
slides.text: The lifecycle keeps going.

slides.headline: The software lifecycle is build, test, ship, maintain — on repeat
slides.text: Software is planned, built, verified, released, then monitored and changed continuously as bugs and needs surface.

slides.headline: Each stage feeds the next, and maintenance loops back to build
slides.text: Requirements shape the build; tests gate the ship; production feedback becomes the next round of requirements. It's a cycle, not a line.

slides.headline: Rushing to ship trades short-term speed for long-term maintenance cost
slides.text: Skipping tests and design gets you live faster and buys you a slower, riskier every-release after that — the debt compounds.

slides.headline: Software is never 'done' — it's shipped, watched, and changed for as long as anyone uses it
slides.text: Launch is the middle of the story, not the end.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Git, GitHub & How Teams Actually Collaborate on Code

posts.title: Git, GitHub & How Teams Actually Collaborate on Code

slides.headline: Two people edited the same file and one of them lost a day of work — before Git
slides.text: Version control exists so that never happens.

slides.headline: Git tracks every change; GitHub hosts it so teams can collaborate
slides.text: Git records snapshots of your code over time and lets branches diverge and merge; GitHub is the shared home where those histories live and get reviewed.

slides.headline: Branch, commit, push, pull request, merge
slides.text: You work on a branch, save changes as commits, push them up, open a pull request for review, and merge once approved — history stays intact and blame is traceable.

slides.headline: Branching enables parallel work but creates merge conflicts to resolve
slides.text: Everyone working independently is the point; the cost is reconciling changes that touched the same lines — conflicts are the tax on parallelism.

slides.headline: Git is a time machine for code; branches let a team edit the same project without overwriting each other
slides.text: Version control turns collaboration from chaos into history.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Clean Code, SOLID & Design Patterns

posts.title: Clean Code, SOLID & Design Patterns

slides.headline: The feature worked, but nobody — including you next month — could safely change it
slides.text: Working code isn't the same as good code.

slides.headline: Clean code, SOLID, and design patterns make code changeable, not just correct
slides.text: Clean code is readable and simple; SOLID is five principles for structuring classes; patterns are reusable solutions to recurring design problems.

slides.headline: Good structure isolates change so one edit doesn't ripple everywhere
slides.text: When responsibilities are separated and dependencies point the right way, a new requirement touches one place instead of ten.

slides.headline: Structure costs upfront effort and buys cheaper future change
slides.text: Applying principles and patterns is slower to write and easier to extend; skipping them is faster today and a tangle tomorrow — and patterns overused become their own mess.

slides.headline: Clean code optimises for the human who edits it next — usually a tired version of you
slides.text: Readability is a feature, not a luxury.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Network Topologies & The Devices That Move Data

posts.title: Network Topologies & The Devices That Move Data

slides.headline: Two computers a metre apart can't talk until you decide how to wire them together
slides.text: That layout has a name: topology.

slides.headline: A topology is the shape of how devices connect; switches and routers move the data
slides.text: Star, mesh, bus — each is a pattern for wiring machines together, and networking hardware forwards traffic along those links.

slides.headline: A switch connects devices in one network; a router connects networks to each other
slides.text: Data hops device-to-switch inside your network, and switch-to-router when it needs to leave for another network.

slides.headline: A mesh survives failures but costs many links; a star is cheap but hinges on one hub
slides.text: Connecting everything to everything is resilient and expensive; connecting everything to a central point is simple and fragile at that point.

slides.headline: Topology is the shape of the network; switches move data within it, routers move it between networks
slides.text: How machines are wired decides how — and whether — they can talk.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: OSI Model, TCP/IP & How Devices Find Each Other

posts.title: OSI Model, TCP/IP & How Devices Find Each Other

slides.headline: A message crossing the internet is handled by a dozen layers you never see
slides.text: Models like OSI make that stack understandable.

slides.headline: The OSI and TCP/IP models split networking into layers, each with one job
slides.text: From physical signals up to the application, each layer handles one concern and hands off to the next — so problems can be isolated to a layer.

slides.headline: Your data gets wrapped by each layer on the way out and unwrapped on the way in
slides.text: The app hands bytes down; each layer adds its own header (addressing, ports, error checks); the receiver peels them off in reverse.

slides.headline: OSI's seven layers teach cleanly; TCP/IP's four layers ship in reality
slides.text: The seven-layer model is a precise teaching tool; the internet actually runs on the leaner TCP/IP stack — the map isn't quite the territory.

slides.headline: Layering means each part of networking solves one problem and trusts the layers around it
slides.text: Complexity becomes manageable when every layer minds its own job.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Do Networks Even Exist?

posts.title: Why Do Networks Even Exist?

slides.headline: One computer is useful; the value explodes the moment two of them can share
slides.text: That's why networks exist.

slides.headline: A network exists to let separate machines share data and resources
slides.text: Instead of copying files by hand, machines exchange them directly — and can share printers, storage, and services too.

slides.headline: Connect machines, agree on rules, and any of them can reach any other
slides.text: Physical links plus shared protocols mean a message can travel from one machine to another it has never directly met.

slides.headline: Networking multiplies capability but adds latency, failure, and attack surface
slides.text: Sharing unlocks everything from email to the cloud; it also means your data now travels links that can be slow, broken, or eavesdropped.

slides.headline: A network turns isolated computers into a system whose value grows with every connection
slides.text: The point of a network is that the whole beats the sum of the machines.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: The Internet's Origin Story: ARPANET to Today

posts.title: The Internet's Origin Story: ARPANET to Today

slides.headline: The internet wasn't designed as one thing — it grew from a small, deliberately fault-tolerant experiment
slides.text: ARPANET is where it started.

slides.headline: The internet began as ARPANET, built to survive partial failure
slides.text: It connected a few research computers with a design goal: if one link died, data should reroute rather than stop.

slides.headline: Packet switching let messages take any working path
slides.text: Instead of a dedicated line, data is chopped into packets that each find their own route and reassemble at the destination — no single point brings it down.

slides.headline: A decentralised design is resilient but has no one in charge
slides.text: No central authority means no single failure or off-switch, and also no single body that can guarantee performance or fix everything.

slides.headline: The internet is robust because it was built to route around damage, not to be controlled from the centre
slides.text: Its resilience is a design choice from day one.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: IP Addresses, MAC Addresses & Ports Explained

posts.title: IP Addresses, MAC Addresses & Ports Explained

slides.headline: Your laptop has at least two different 'addresses', and they do completely different jobs
slides.text: IP and MAC aren't interchangeable.

slides.headline: IP addresses locate networks; MAC addresses identify devices; ports identify apps
slides.text: An IP says which machine on which network; a MAC is the hardware's fixed identity on the local link; a port says which program on that machine.

slides.headline: Data is delivered by IP across networks, by MAC on the final hop, to the right port
slides.text: Routers forward by IP until the last network, where MAC delivers to the exact device, and the port hands it to the right application.

slides.headline: IP can change with location; MAC is burned into the hardware
slides.text: Your IP shifts as you move between networks; your MAC stays the same — one is a mailing address, the other a fingerprint.

slides.headline: IP finds the network, MAC finds the device, the port finds the app — three addresses, three scopes
slides.text: Delivery on the internet is three questions answered in order.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: TCP vs UDP: The Protocols Behind Every Connection

posts.title: TCP vs UDP: The Protocols Behind Every Connection

slides.headline: A video call and a file download both cross the same wire, but they want opposite things
slides.text: So they use different protocols.

slides.headline: TCP guarantees delivery in order; UDP just fires packets and moves on
slides.text: TCP checks that every packet arrives and reassembles them correctly; UDP sends without confirmation, accepting that some may be lost.

slides.headline: TCP handshakes, acknowledges, and retransmits; UDP skips all of it
slides.text: TCP sets up a connection and confirms each chunk, adding round-trips; UDP has no setup and no acknowledgements, so it's leaner but lossy.

slides.headline: TCP: reliable but slower. UDP: fast but lossy.
slides.text: Downloads and web pages need every byte, so they use TCP; live video and games prefer fresh data over complete data, so they use UDP and tolerate drops.

slides.headline: TCP promises every packet arrives in order; UDP promises speed and nothing else
slides.text: Reliability or latency — the protocol is the choice.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: DNS & DHCP: How Devices Find Each Other

posts.title: DNS & DHCP: How Devices Find Each Other

slides.headline: You type a name, not an address — and something silently gets you a phone number for the internet
slides.text: That's DNS at work.

slides.headline: DNS turns names into IP addresses; DHCP hands out addresses automatically
slides.text: DNS is the internet's phone book, resolving google.com to an IP; DHCP is what assigns your device its own IP the moment it joins a network.

slides.headline: Join a network, DHCP gives you an address; visit a site, DNS resolves its name
slides.text: Your device asks DHCP for a local IP, then asks DNS to translate each domain you visit into the server's IP so it can connect.

slides.headline: Caching DNS makes browsing fast but can serve stale records
slides.text: Resolved names are remembered for speed, so you don't look up google.com every time — but a changed IP can linger in caches until they expire.

slides.headline: DNS is the internet's phone book; DHCP is the desk that hands you a number when you walk in
slides.text: Names for humans, numbers for machines, translated automatically.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Routers, Switches, NAT & Firewalls

posts.title: Routers, Switches, NAT & Firewalls

slides.headline: Your home has one public IP, but a dozen devices reach the internet through it at once
slides.text: NAT is quietly making that work.

slides.headline: Routers, switches, NAT, and firewalls together move and guard traffic
slides.text: Switches connect local devices, routers connect networks, NAT lets many devices share one public IP, and firewalls decide what traffic is allowed.

slides.headline: NAT rewrites addresses so private devices can share one public identity
slides.text: Outgoing traffic gets the router's public IP and a tracked port; replies are mapped back to the right internal device — many hidden behind one.

slides.headline: NAT conserves addresses and hides devices, but complicates direct incoming connections
slides.text: It stretched a limited IP supply and adds a layer of obscurity; it also makes it harder for outside machines to initiate a connection inward.

slides.headline: A router directs, NAT translates, a firewall filters — the trio that lets a private network face the internet safely
slides.text: Sharing one address and staying guarded is the everyday job of your router.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: HTTP, HTTPS & TLS: How the Web Stays (Somewhat) Secure

posts.title: HTTP, HTTPS & TLS: How the Web Stays (Somewhat) Secure

slides.headline: The 's' in https isn't cosmetic — without it, anyone on the network can read your login
slides.text: That letter is TLS.

slides.headline: HTTP carries web requests; HTTPS wraps them in TLS encryption
slides.text: HTTP is the plain protocol browsers and servers speak; HTTPS is the same protocol run inside an encrypted TLS tunnel.

slides.headline: TLS verifies the server's identity, then encrypts everything after
slides.text: A handshake checks the site's certificate and agrees on keys; from then on, requests and responses are scrambled to anyone in between.

slides.headline: HTTPS adds a handshake and CPU cost to buy privacy and integrity
slides.text: The extra setup and encryption cost a little latency and compute; in return, traffic can't be read or tampered with in transit — nearly always worth it.

slides.headline: HTTPS is HTTP inside a locked tunnel — same messages, but no one in the middle can read them
slides.text: Encryption is what makes the web safe to log in to.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Really Happens When You Type google.com

posts.title: What Really Happens When You Type google.com

slides.headline: You type google.com and hit enter — in under a second, a dozen systems cooperate
slides.text: Here's the whole chain.

slides.headline: One URL triggers DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, and rendering in sequence
slides.text: The name is resolved, a connection is opened and secured, a request is sent, a response comes back, and the browser paints it.

slides.headline: Resolve, connect, secure, request, respond, render
slides.text: DNS finds the IP, TCP opens the connection, TLS encrypts it, HTTP asks for the page, the server responds, and the browser turns the response into pixels.

slides.headline: Each step is fast alone but they add up, so caching cuts the repeats
slides.text: DNS answers, connections, and assets get cached so the second visit skips most of the chain — the cost is possibly serving something slightly stale.

slides.headline: Loading a web page is a relay race across DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP — every runner has to finish
slides.text: One address quietly sets a whole stack in motion.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: HTML: The Skeleton of Every Website

posts.title: HTML: The Skeleton of Every Website

slides.headline: Turn off CSS and JavaScript and a website is still there — just bare
slides.text: That skeleton is HTML.

slides.headline: HTML defines the structure and meaning of a page, not its looks
slides.text: Headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images — HTML says what each piece of content is, in a tree of nested elements.

slides.headline: The browser parses HTML into a tree it can display and script
slides.text: Tags become nodes in the DOM; that tree is what CSS styles and JavaScript manipulates later.

slides.headline: Semantic HTML costs a little discipline and pays back in accessibility and SEO
slides.text: Using the right element (nav, article, button) instead of generic divs takes thought, but screen readers and search engines rely on that meaning.

slides.headline: HTML is the skeleton — it decides what's on the page, before anything decides how it looks
slides.text: Structure first; style and behaviour come after.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: CSS: Making the Web Actually Look Good

posts.title: CSS: Making the Web Actually Look Good

slides.headline: The same HTML can look like a spreadsheet or a magazine — CSS is the difference
slides.text: Style lives entirely outside the structure.

slides.headline: CSS controls how HTML looks: layout, colour, spacing, type
slides.text: It's a separate language of rules that select elements and describe their appearance and position.

slides.headline: Selectors target elements; the box model and layout systems position them
slides.text: You point at elements with selectors, then use the box model, flexbox, or grid to control size, spacing, and arrangement.

slides.headline: Separating style from structure keeps both clean but adds specificity puzzles
slides.text: Splitting looks from content means you can restyle without touching HTML; the cost is cascade and specificity rules that decide which conflicting style wins.

slides.headline: HTML says what it is; CSS says how it looks — keep the two jobs apart and both stay sane
slides.text: Presentation is a separate concern from meaning.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: JavaScript Basics: Making Pages Interactive

posts.title: JavaScript Basics: Making Pages Interactive

slides.headline: HTML and CSS give you a page that just sits there — clicking anything does nothing
slides.text: JavaScript is what makes it react.

slides.headline: JavaScript adds behaviour: it responds to events and changes the page live
slides.text: It runs in the browser, listens for clicks and input, and updates the DOM without reloading.

slides.headline: An event fires, your code runs, the DOM changes, the user sees it
slides.text: A button click triggers a function; that function reads or rewrites the page's elements; the browser re-renders the affected part.

slides.headline: More interactivity means more client-side code to load, run, and maintain
slides.text: Rich behaviour improves the experience but ships more script to every visitor and adds state that can get out of sync with the page.

slides.headline: HTML and CSS build the page; JavaScript is what lets it respond to the person using it
slides.text: Structure, style, then behaviour — the third layer brings it alive.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Closures, Promises & Async/Await: JS Gets Real

posts.title: Closures, Promises & Async/Await: JS Gets Real

slides.headline: Your code asks for data, then immediately uses it — and gets 'undefined'
slides.text: The data hadn't arrived yet. Welcome to async.

slides.headline: Closures capture state; promises and async/await handle work that finishes later
slides.text: A closure remembers the variables around it; a promise represents a value that isn't ready yet; async/await lets you write that waiting as if it were sequential.

slides.headline: Kick off slow work, keep going, and handle the result when it lands
slides.text: Instead of freezing while a network request runs, JavaScript registers what to do when it completes and moves on — then resumes with the result.

slides.headline: Async keeps the UI responsive but makes control flow harder to follow
slides.text: Non-blocking code means the page never freezes on a slow call; the cost is reasoning about code that doesn't run top-to-bottom in order.

slides.headline: A promise is an IOU for a value; async/await lets you wait for it without freezing everything else
slides.text: Asynchrony trades linear reading for a responsive program.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Fetch, APIs & JS Modules

posts.title: Fetch, APIs & JS Modules

slides.headline: A modern web app is mostly your page asking other servers for data, constantly
slides.text: fetch is how it asks.

slides.headline: fetch calls APIs; modules organise JS into reusable, isolated files
slides.text: fetch sends HTTP requests from the browser and returns a promise; ES modules let you split code into files that explicitly import and export what they share.

slides.headline: Request data, await the response, parse it, update the page
slides.text: Your code fetches from an API endpoint, waits for the JSON, turns it into objects, and renders them — no page reload needed.

slides.headline: Splitting into modules improves clarity but adds build and dependency complexity
slides.text: Small, focused files are easier to reason about and reuse; the trade is a build step and a dependency graph to manage.

slides.headline: fetch is how the browser talks to servers; modules are how you keep the code that does it organised
slides.text: The modern front end is requests and reusable pieces.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Library vs Framework: Why React Exists

posts.title: Library vs Framework: Why React Exists

slides.headline: You can build a UI with plain JavaScript — until the app grows and the manual DOM updates become unmanageable
slides.text: That's the gap frameworks fill.

slides.headline: A library you call; a framework calls you — React sits in between and owns the rendering
slides.text: With a library, your code is in charge; a framework provides the structure and runs your code within it. React manages when and how the UI updates.

slides.headline: You describe the UI for a given state; React updates the DOM to match
slides.text: Instead of manually changing elements, you write what the page should look like for the current data, and React figures out the minimal DOM changes.

slides.headline: A framework saves boilerplate but imposes its conventions and learning curve
slides.text: You write far less repetitive UI code and gain structure; you also buy into its way of doing things and its update cycle.

slides.headline: A library is a tool you pick up; a framework is a house you move into — React trades freedom for structure
slides.text: You give up manual control to stop managing the DOM by hand.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: State, Routing & Server-Side Rendering

posts.title: State, Routing & Server-Side Rendering

slides.headline: Your app remembers what the user did, shows the right page, and loads fast on first paint
slides.text: State, routing, and rendering strategy are doing that.

slides.headline: State is the app's live data; routing maps URLs to views; SSR renders on the server first
slides.text: State drives what's shown; routing decides which component a URL displays; server-side rendering sends ready-made HTML before the JS loads.

slides.headline: Server renders the first view, the browser takes over, state drives everything after
slides.text: SSR delivers a fast, visible page; then client-side code hydrates it and manages state and navigation without full reloads.

slides.headline: SSR improves first load and SEO but costs server work; client rendering is lighter on the server but slower to first paint
slides.text: Rendering on the server gets content visible sooner and crawlable; doing it in the browser offloads the server but shows a blank page longer.

slides.headline: State is what changes, routing is where you are, SSR is who draws the first frame — the three levers of a modern app
slides.text: Where and when you render is an architecture decision, not a detail.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Node.js & Express: JavaScript on the Backend

posts.title: Node.js & Express: JavaScript on the Backend

slides.headline: JavaScript was trapped in the browser for years — then Node let it run the server too
slides.text: Now one language spans both ends.

slides.headline: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser; Express structures the server code
slides.text: Node gives JS access to files, networks, and the OS; Express is a minimal framework for defining routes and handling HTTP requests on top of it.

slides.headline: A request hits a route, your handler runs, a response goes back
slides.text: Express matches the URL and method to a handler function; that function does the work — query a database, shape data — and returns a response.

slides.headline: One language across the stack speeds teams up but Node's single thread punishes heavy CPU work
slides.text: Sharing JS front-to-back reduces context switching; Node's event loop shines at many I/O tasks and stalls on one heavy computation.

slides.headline: Node put JavaScript on the server; Express gave it a clean way to answer requests
slides.text: The browser language became a full-stack language.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: REST APIs, Auth & Authorization Explained

posts.title: REST APIs, Auth & Authorization Explained

slides.headline: Your app needs to let the right people do the right things — and block everyone else
slides.text: That's auth, and it's two separate questions.

slides.headline: A REST API exposes resources over HTTP; authentication is who you are, authorization is what you may do
slides.text: REST maps URLs to resources and verbs to actions; authentication proves identity; authorization checks permissions.

slides.headline: Verify the user, then check whether that user is allowed this action
slides.text: First confirm identity (login, token); then, on each request, decide if this identity has the right to the resource — two checks, in order.

slides.headline: Confusing authentication with authorization is a classic, dangerous bug
slides.text: Proving someone is logged in isn't the same as proving they may delete this record; skip the second check and any user can act as any other.

slides.headline: Authentication asks 'who are you?'; authorization asks 'are you allowed?' — never merge the two
slides.text: Identity and permission are different gates.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Cookies, Sessions, JWT, Middleware & WebSockets

posts.title: Cookies, Sessions, JWT, Middleware & WebSockets

slides.headline: HTTP forgets you the instant a request ends — so how does a site keep you logged in?
slides.text: With one of several ways to carry state.

slides.headline: Cookies, sessions, and JWTs carry identity across stateless requests; middleware and WebSockets extend the server
slides.text: A cookie stores a token in the browser; a session keeps state on the server; a JWT is a signed, self-contained token. Middleware processes requests in a pipeline; WebSockets keep a connection open for real-time data.

slides.headline: Log in once, get a token, send it with every later request
slides.text: The server issues a session ID or JWT; the browser returns it on each request so the server recognises you without asking again.

slides.headline: Server sessions are easy to revoke but hold state; JWTs scale statelessly but are hard to invalidate early
slides.text: Sessions can be killed instantly but need shared storage; JWTs need no lookup and scale well, but a leaked token stays valid until it expires.

slides.headline: HTTP is forgetful; cookies, sessions, and tokens are how a site remembers you between requests
slides.text: Statelessness is the default — identity is something you carry back each time.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Do We Even Need Databases?

posts.title: Why Do We Even Need Databases?

slides.headline: You could store everything in files — until two users write at once and the data corrupts
slides.text: That's the problem databases solve.

slides.headline: A database stores data with structure, safety, and fast querying
slides.text: It handles concurrent access, prevents corruption, enforces rules, and lets you retrieve exactly what you need quickly — things raw files don't.

slides.headline: Many clients read and write at once; the database keeps it consistent
slides.text: It coordinates simultaneous access, so two users updating the same record don't overwrite each other or leave the data half-changed.

slides.headline: A database adds power and safety but also a system to run and learn
slides.text: Files are simple and portable; a database buys querying, integrity, and concurrency at the cost of setup, operation, and a query language to learn.

slides.headline: A database is a file that knows how to be shared, queried, and kept correct under pressure
slides.text: When many users touch the same data, structure stops being optional.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Tables, Keys & Relationships: The Relational Model

posts.title: Tables, Keys & Relationships: The Relational Model

slides.headline: A spreadsheet works until the same customer's name is spelled three ways in three places
slides.text: The relational model fixes that.

slides.headline: The relational model organises data into tables linked by keys
slides.text: Each table holds one kind of thing; a primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key points from one table to another to model relationships.

slides.headline: Store each fact once, then connect tables through keys
slides.text: A customer lives in one row of one table; orders reference that customer by key — update the name once and every order stays correct.

slides.headline: Normalising removes duplication but adds joins to reassemble data
slides.text: Splitting data into related tables prevents inconsistency; the cost is that answering a question often means joining several tables back together.

slides.headline: The relational model stores each fact once and links the rest with keys
slides.text: No duplication means no contradictions.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: SQL, JOINs & Indexes Explained

posts.title: SQL, JOINs & Indexes Explained

slides.headline: Your query returned the right rows and took eight seconds — the same query with an index takes eight milliseconds
slides.text: JOINs and indexes are why.

slides.headline: SQL queries data; JOINs combine tables; indexes make lookups fast
slides.text: SQL describes what data you want; a JOIN stitches related tables together; an index is a sorted lookup structure that avoids scanning every row.

slides.headline: Without an index, the database reads every row; with one, it jumps straight there
slides.text: An index is like a book's index — instead of reading all pages to find a term, the database goes directly to matching rows.

slides.headline: Indexes speed reads but slow writes and use space
slides.text: Every index makes matching queries fast; it also has to be updated on every insert and update and takes storage — index the columns you filter on, not everything.

slides.headline: A JOIN reassembles what normalisation split; an index is the shortcut that stops the database reading everything
slides.text: Query the shape you stored, and index the columns you search.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Transactions, ACID & Concurrency

posts.title: Transactions, ACID & Concurrency

slides.headline: A transfer debited one account and crashed before crediting the other — money vanished
slides.text: Transactions exist so that can't happen.

slides.headline: A transaction groups operations so they all succeed or all fail; ACID defines the guarantees
slides.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: all-or-nothing, valid states only, isolated from other transactions, and permanent once committed.

slides.headline: Wrap related writes in a transaction; commit together or roll back together
slides.text: The debit and credit run inside one transaction — if anything fails, both are undone, so the account balances never end up half-updated.

slides.headline: Stronger isolation prevents concurrency bugs but reduces throughput
slides.text: Higher isolation levels stop transactions from seeing each other's half-done work; they also force more locking and waiting, cutting how much runs in parallel.

slides.headline: A transaction is all-or-nothing — the operations commit together or leave no trace
slides.text: ACID is the promise that half-finished work never becomes reality.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: SQL vs NoSQL: Postgres, MongoDB & Redis

posts.title: SQL vs NoSQL: Postgres, MongoDB & Redis

slides.headline: 'Just use a database' hides a real fork: rigid-and-consistent, or flexible-and-fast?
slides.text: SQL and NoSQL answer it differently.

slides.headline: SQL databases enforce a schema and strong consistency; NoSQL trades some of that for scale and flexibility
slides.text: Postgres is relational and strict; MongoDB stores flexible documents; Redis is an in-memory key-value store built for speed.

slides.headline: Pick by the shape of your data and what you can't compromise on
slides.text: Structured, related data with strict correctness leans SQL; loosely-structured or massive, high-throughput data leans NoSQL — often you use both.

slides.headline: SQL: consistency and rich queries. NoSQL: flexibility and horizontal scale.
slides.text: Relational databases give you joins, transactions, and guarantees; NoSQL stores scale out easily and bend to changing data, but often relax consistency and cross-record queries.

slides.headline: SQL is strict and relational; NoSQL is flexible and scalable — match the store to what the data can't give up
slides.text: There's no default winner, only a fit to your constraints.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Security Isn't Optional

posts.title: Why Security Isn't Optional

slides.headline: Security feels optional right up until the breach — then it's the only thing anyone talks about
slides.text: It's cheaper as a habit than a cleanup.

slides.headline: Security is protecting data and systems from misuse, guided by threat, vulnerability, and exploit
slides.text: A threat is who might attack; a vulnerability is the weakness they target; an exploit is the act of using it. Defense addresses all three.

slides.headline: Assume inputs are hostile, limit what each part can do, and defend in layers
slides.text: Validate everything from outside, give components only the access they need, and stack defenses so one failure isn't total.

slides.headline: Every convenience you add is potential attack surface
slides.text: More features, integrations, and access make software friendlier and give attackers more doors — security is the discipline of closing the ones you don't need.

slides.headline: Security isn't a feature you bolt on — it's assuming every input is hostile until proven safe
slides.text: Treat trust as something earned, not granted by default.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Encryption Explained: Symmetric vs Asymmetric

posts.title: Encryption Explained: Symmetric vs Asymmetric

slides.headline: How do two people who've never met agree on a secret over a wire everyone can read?
slides.text: Asymmetric encryption pulls it off.

slides.headline: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
slides.text: With symmetric, the same key locks and unlocks — fast, but both sides must already share it. With asymmetric, anyone can encrypt with your public key, but only your private key decrypts.

slides.headline: Use asymmetric to exchange a key safely, then symmetric to move data fast
slides.text: Public-key crypto lets strangers agree on a shared secret over an open channel; that secret then powers fast symmetric encryption for the bulk of the traffic.

slides.headline: Symmetric is fast but needs a pre-shared key; asymmetric solves key exchange but is slow
slides.text: One is quick and awkward to set up; the other bootstraps trust between strangers but is too slow for large data — so real systems combine them.

slides.headline: Asymmetric crypto lets strangers agree on a secret in the open; symmetric crypto makes using it fast
slides.text: Public keys start the conversation; shared keys carry it.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Password Security & the Attacks Every Dev Should Know

posts.title: Password Security & the Attacks Every Dev Should Know

slides.headline: A leaked database dumped millions of passwords in plain text — because someone stored them raw
slides.text: That's the mistake hashing prevents.

slides.headline: Never store passwords directly — store slow, salted hashes
slides.text: A hash is a one-way fingerprint; a salt makes each one unique; a deliberately slow algorithm makes guessing expensive.

slides.headline: Hash on the way in, compare hashes on login, never keep the original
slides.text: When a user sets a password you store only its salted hash; at login you hash the attempt and compare — the real password is never saved.

slides.headline: Slow hashing frustrates attackers at a tiny cost to honest logins
slides.text: A deliberately slow algorithm barely affects one real login but makes brute-forcing billions of guesses impractical — friction aimed only at attackers.

slides.headline: Store the fingerprint, never the password — salted and slow, so a breach leaks nothing usable
slides.text: If your database can reveal a password, you've already lost.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Rate Limiting, Secrets & OAuth

posts.title: Rate Limiting, Secrets & OAuth

slides.headline: One leaked API key or one unthrottled endpoint can undo every other precaution
slides.text: Rate limiting, secrets, and OAuth close those gaps.

slides.headline: Rate limiting caps abuse, secrets management guards credentials, OAuth delegates access safely
slides.text: Rate limits stop brute-force and overload; secrets are kept out of code and rotated; OAuth lets an app act for a user without handling their password.

slides.headline: Throttle requests, keep secrets out of the codebase, and hand out scoped tokens
slides.text: Limit how often a client can call you; store keys in a vault or environment, not source; issue OAuth tokens that grant only specific permissions.

slides.headline: OAuth avoids sharing passwords but adds real flow complexity
slides.text: Delegated access means users never give one app their credentials for another; the cost is a multi-step token flow that's easy to misconfigure.

slides.headline: Rate limits slow attackers, secret management hides the keys, OAuth shares access without sharing passwords
slides.text: The last mile of security is guarding credentials and access, not just data.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Linux & the Command Line Every Server Speaks

posts.title: Linux & the Command Line Every Server Speaks

slides.headline: Every server you'll ever deploy to speaks the same language — and it isn't a GUI
slides.text: It's the Linux command line.

slides.headline: The Linux CLI controls the machine directly; processes and services are what's running
slides.text: Commands manipulate files, processes, and permissions; a process is a running program; a service is a process the system keeps running in the background.

slides.headline: Type a command, the shell runs it as a process, output comes back
slides.text: The shell interprets your command, launches it as a process with your permissions, and streams its output — the same loop whether local or over SSH.

slides.headline: The CLI is unforgiving but scriptable and remote-friendly
slides.text: A GUI is easier to explore; the command line is faster, automatable, and works over a text connection to a server with no screen — which is where software actually runs.

slides.headline: The command line is how you actually run and control the servers your software lives on
slides.text: Comfort with the shell is comfort with production.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is DevOps, Really? The Culture Behind the Tools

posts.title: What Is DevOps, Really? The Culture Behind the Tools

slides.headline: Devs wanted to ship fast; ops wanted things stable — DevOps exists to end that war
slides.text: It's a culture before it's a toolset.

slides.headline: DevOps unites development and operations; CALMS and the Three Ways frame the mindset
slides.text: CALMS is Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing. The Three Ways are flow, feedback, and continual learning — principles, not products.

slides.headline: Automate the path from commit to production and shorten every feedback loop
slides.text: Instead of throwing code over a wall, one pipeline builds, tests, and deploys, and telemetry feeds problems back fast.

slides.headline: DevOps trades upfront automation effort for faster, safer, repeatable releases
slides.text: Building pipelines and culture takes real investment; it pays back as deployments become routine, frequent, and low-drama instead of rare and terrifying.

slides.headline: DevOps is a culture of automating flow and feedback, not a tool you install
slides.text: The tools serve the principle: ship faster by making shipping boring.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Logs, SSH & Shell Scripting

posts.title: Logs, SSH & Shell Scripting

slides.headline: When production breaks at 3am, you have no GUI, one SSH connection, and the logs
slides.text: Those three skills are the toolkit.

slides.headline: Logs record what happened; SSH gets you onto the server; shell scripts automate the routine
