slides.text: Logs are the system's diary for debugging; SSH is an encrypted remote shell; scripts turn repeated command sequences into one reusable file.

slides.headline: SSH in, read the logs, script the fix so you never do it by hand again
slides.text: You connect remotely, tail the logs to find the failure, then capture the recovery steps in a script for next time.

slides.headline: Scripting a task costs time now and saves it every repeat after
slides.text: Writing a script is slower than doing the thing once; it pays off the second, tenth, and hundredth time — and removes human error from the routine.

slides.headline: Logs tell you what broke, SSH gets you there, scripts make sure you fix it only once
slides.text: Operations is turning firefighting into automation.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Nginx & What Deployment Actually Means

posts.title: Nginx & What Deployment Actually Means

slides.headline: Your app runs on your laptop — 'deployment' is the messy gap between that and users reaching it
slides.text: Nginx sits right in that gap.

slides.headline: Deployment is making your app reachable in production; Nginx fronts it as a web server and reverse proxy
slides.text: Deploying means running your code on a server the public can reach; Nginx receives incoming requests and forwards them to your app, serving static files directly.

slides.headline: Requests hit Nginx first, which routes, serves, or forwards them
slides.text: Nginx terminates connections, hands static assets straight back, and passes dynamic requests to your application — shielding it from the raw internet.

slides.headline: A reverse proxy adds a hop but buys TLS, load balancing, and buffering
slides.text: Putting Nginx in front adds one layer to manage; in return you get a single place for HTTPS, routing, caching, and spreading load across app instances.

slides.headline: Deployment is the leap from 'runs on my machine' to 'reachable by anyone'; Nginx guards the front door
slides.text: Getting live is a system, not a copy-paste.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Docker: Containers, Images & Your First Dockerfile

posts.title: Docker: Containers, Images & Your First Dockerfile

slides.headline: 'It works on my machine' died the day containers arrived
slides.text: Docker packages the machine with the app.

slides.headline: A container bundles your app with everything it needs to run, identically anywhere
slides.text: An image is the frozen bundle of code, dependencies, and config; a container is a running instance of it; a Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image.

slides.headline: Write a Dockerfile, build an image, run it as a container
slides.text: You declare the base, dependencies, and start command; Docker builds a portable image; that image runs the same on any machine with Docker.

slides.headline: Containers are lighter than VMs but share the host kernel
slides.text: Unlike a full virtual machine, containers don't boot their own OS — they're fast and small, but isolated less completely because they share the host's kernel.

slides.headline: A container ships the environment with the app, so 'works on my machine' becomes 'works everywhere'
slides.text: Package the whole context, not just the code.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Docker Volumes, Networking & Compose

posts.title: Docker Volumes, Networking & Compose

slides.headline: Kill a container and its data is gone; run three and they can't find each other
slides.text: Volumes persist the data and Docker networks let containers reach each other — Compose wires it all up in one file.

slides.headline: Volumes persist data, Docker networks let containers talk, Compose orchestrates multiple containers
slides.text: A container's filesystem is disposable, so volumes store data outside it; container networks give them addresses to reach each other; Compose defines a whole multi-container app in one file.

slides.headline: Declare services, volumes, and a network once; bring the stack up together
slides.text: A Compose file lists your app, database, and cache, their shared network, and their persistent volumes — one command starts the lot, wired correctly.

slides.headline: Compose is great for one host but isn't a cluster orchestrator
slides.text: It's ideal for local dev and single-server stacks; it doesn't handle scheduling across many machines — that's where Kubernetes takes over.

slides.headline: Volumes keep the data, networks connect the containers, Compose brings the whole stack up at once
slides.text: Containers become a system when they can persist, talk, and start together.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Container Registries & CI/CD

posts.title: Container Registries & CI/CD

slides.headline: You built an image locally — now every server and teammate needs the same one, automatically
slides.text: Registries and CI/CD close that loop.

slides.headline: A registry stores and shares images; CI/CD automates build, test, and deploy
slides.text: A container registry is the shared home for images; CI/CD is a pipeline that, on every code change, builds the image, runs tests, and ships it.

slides.headline: Push code, the pipeline builds and tests, then deploys the image from the registry
slides.text: A commit triggers CI to build and test; if it passes, the image is pushed to the registry and pulled into production — no manual steps.

slides.headline: Automated pipelines cost setup and catch problems before users do
slides.text: Building CI/CD takes real configuration effort; it pays back by making releases frequent, tested, and reversible instead of rare and risky.

slides.headline: A registry shares the image; CI/CD is the conveyor belt from commit to production
slides.text: Automate the path to prod and shipping stops being an event.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Monitoring, Alerting & Distributed Tracing: Prometheus, Grafana & Jaeger

posts.title: Monitoring, Alerting & Distributed Tracing: Prometheus, Grafana & Jaeger

slides.headline: In a system of twenty services, 'it's slow' is useless — slow where?
slides.text: Monitoring, alerting, and tracing answer that.

slides.headline: Metrics show health, alerts warn you, traces follow one request across services
slides.text: Prometheus collects metrics, Grafana visualises them, alerts fire on thresholds, and Jaeger traces a single request as it hops between services.

slides.headline: Collect metrics, chart them, alert on trouble, trace the slow request end to end
slides.text: Services emit metrics Prometheus scrapes; Grafana graphs them; an alert fires when something breaches a limit; a trace reveals which hop actually caused the delay.

slides.headline: More observability costs storage and overhead but slashes time-to-diagnose
slides.text: Instrumenting everything generates data to store and process; it turns 'we're guessing' into 'we can see exactly where it broke' — usually a bargain in an outage.

slides.headline: Metrics say something's wrong, alerts wake you, traces point at the exact hop that failed
slides.text: You can't fix what you can't see — observability is that sight.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Infrastructure as Code & Config Management: Terraform & Ansible

posts.title: Infrastructure as Code & Config Management: Terraform & Ansible

slides.headline: Someone configured the server by hand, left, and now nobody can rebuild it
slides.text: Infrastructure as code makes that impossible.

slides.headline: IaC and config management define infrastructure in version-controlled files
slides.text: Terraform declares what infrastructure should exist; Ansible configures what's on each machine — both from files you commit, not clicks you remember.

slides.headline: Describe the desired state in code; the tool makes reality match it
slides.text: You write the servers, networks, and settings you want; the tool compares that to what exists and creates or changes only what's needed to converge.

slides.headline: Declarative infrastructure is reproducible but adds a layer to learn and maintain
slides.text: Defining infra in code makes it reviewable, versioned, and rebuildable anywhere; the cost is learning the tools and keeping state in sync with reality.

slides.headline: Infrastructure as code turns 'the one server someone set up' into a file anyone can rebuild
slides.text: If it isn't in code, it's a single point of failure named a person.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Service Mesh: Istio & Service-to-Service Communication

posts.title: Service Mesh: Istio & Service-to-Service Communication

slides.headline: With fifty services, each reinventing retries, TLS, and routing, the duplication becomes the bug
slides.text: A service mesh moves that out of your code.

slides.headline: A service mesh handles service-to-service communication outside your application
slides.text: It puts a proxy beside each service (a sidecar) that manages retries, encryption, routing, and observability — Istio is a common implementation.

slides.headline: Traffic between services flows through sidecars that enforce the rules
slides.text: Your service just calls another; the mesh's proxies transparently add mTLS, retries, timeouts, and metrics without a line of app code.

slides.headline: A mesh centralises cross-cutting concerns but adds real operational complexity
slides.text: Pulling retries, security, and routing into the platform keeps services simple and consistent; running the mesh itself is a significant new system to operate.

slides.headline: A service mesh moves retries, encryption, and routing out of every service and into the network layer
slides.text: Stop reimplementing plumbing in each service — push it beneath them.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Cloud Computing Exists

posts.title: Why Cloud Computing Exists

slides.headline: You needed 100 servers for one day of traffic, then never again — buying them was madness
slides.text: The cloud exists so you don't have to.

slides.headline: Cloud computing rents computing on demand instead of owning hardware
slides.text: You use someone else's data centres and pay for what you consume, scaling up and down instead of buying for peak.

slides.headline: Request resources, use them, release them, pay by usage
slides.text: Spin up servers, storage, or databases in minutes via an API; shut them down when done; the bill tracks actual consumption.

slides.headline: Renting trades ownership and control for elasticity and no upfront cost
slides.text: Owning hardware is cheaper at steady scale and fully yours; renting is instant, elastic, and someone else's problem to maintain — a great fit for spiky or uncertain demand.

slides.headline: The cloud turns computers from a purchase into a utility you rent by the second
slides.text: Pay for the peak only when you're at it.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Regions, Availability Zones & Data Centers

posts.title: Regions, Availability Zones & Data Centers

slides.headline: Your data centre in Virginia is useless to a user in Tokyo — and if it floods, so is everything
slides.text: Regions and zones exist for exactly this.

slides.headline: Regions are geographic locations; availability zones are isolated data centres within them
slides.text: A region is a part of the world; each region has multiple availability zones — separate facilities with independent power and network, close enough to work as one.

slides.headline: Put users' data near them, and spread copies across zones for safety
slides.text: Choose a region close to your users for low latency; deploy across several zones so one data centre failing doesn't take you down.

slides.headline: Spreading across zones adds cost and complexity but survives a data-centre failure
slides.text: Running in multiple zones or regions costs more and complicates deployment; it's what keeps you online when one facility loses power or connectivity.

slides.headline: Regions put you near users; availability zones keep you alive when one data centre dies
slides.text: Geography and redundancy are architecture decisions, not afterthoughts.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: AWS Basics: EC2, S3 & IAM

posts.title: AWS Basics: EC2, S3 & IAM

slides.headline: Three services underpin most of AWS, and a fourth quietly decides who can touch them
slides.text: EC2, S3, and IAM.

slides.headline: EC2 gives you servers, S3 stores files, IAM controls who can do what
slides.text: EC2 is rentable virtual machines; S3 is durable object storage for files of any size; IAM defines identities and their permissions across everything.

slides.headline: Run compute on EC2, keep data in S3, and gate all of it with IAM
slides.text: Your app runs on EC2 instances, reads and writes assets to S3, and every action is allowed or denied by IAM policies.

slides.headline: Fine-grained IAM is powerful but easy to misconfigure into a breach
slides.text: Precise permissions let you grant exactly what's needed; the same flexibility makes over-permissive policies a leading cause of cloud security incidents.

slides.headline: EC2 is the compute, S3 is the storage, IAM is the bouncer deciding who gets in
slides.text: On AWS, permissions are as load-bearing as the servers.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: VPC, Load Balancers & Auto Scaling

posts.title: VPC, Load Balancers & Auto Scaling

slides.headline: One server behind your app is a single point of failure and a traffic ceiling
slides.text: VPCs, load balancers, and auto scaling remove both.

slides.headline: A VPC is your private network; a load balancer spreads traffic; auto scaling adjusts capacity
slides.text: The VPC isolates your resources; the load balancer distributes requests across instances; auto scaling adds or removes instances as demand changes.

slides.headline: Traffic enters the load balancer, fans out to instances, which scale with demand
slides.text: Requests hit the balancer, which routes them to healthy instances; when load rises, auto scaling launches more; when it falls, it removes them.

slides.headline: Auto scaling absorbs spikes but reacts on a delay and can mask inefficiency
slides.text: It keeps you responsive without over-provisioning; it also takes minutes to react to sudden surges and can quietly paper over code that simply uses too many resources.

slides.headline: A load balancer spreads the load, auto scaling grows the fleet — together they kill the single point of failure
slides.text: Resilience and elasticity are wired into the network, not hoped for.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: RDS, Lambda & CloudWatch

posts.title: RDS, Lambda & CloudWatch

slides.headline: You can run everything on servers you manage — or hand the boring parts to the cloud
slides.text: RDS, Lambda, and CloudWatch are that hand-off.

slides.headline: RDS manages databases, Lambda runs code without servers, CloudWatch watches it all
slides.text: RDS runs and maintains your database for you; Lambda executes functions on demand with no server to manage; CloudWatch collects logs and metrics.

slides.headline: An event triggers a Lambda, which uses RDS, while CloudWatch records everything
slides.text: A request or event invokes a function; it reads or writes the managed database; metrics and logs stream to CloudWatch for monitoring and alerts.

slides.headline: Serverless removes ops but adds cold starts and vendor lock-in
slides.text: Lambda means no servers to patch and pay-per-invocation billing; the trade is startup latency on idle functions and code shaped tightly around one provider.

slides.headline: Managed services trade control for convenience — you stop running the plumbing and start paying per use
slides.text: Let the cloud own the undifferentiated work.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: CDN, Infrastructure as Code & Production Architecture

posts.title: CDN, Infrastructure as Code & Production Architecture

slides.headline: A global product can't serve every user from one region and can't be rebuilt by hand after an outage
slides.text: CDNs and IaC are how real production is run.

slides.headline: A CDN caches content near users; IaC defines the whole architecture as code
slides.text: A content delivery network serves assets from edge locations close to each user; infrastructure as code declares your entire cloud setup in reproducible files.

slides.headline: Cache static content at the edge and define everything else in code
slides.text: Static assets are pushed to edge servers worldwide for fast delivery; the servers, networks, and databases behind them are all declared in Terraform or similar.

slides.headline: A CDN cuts latency but can serve stale content until caches expire
slides.text: Edge caching makes global delivery fast; the cost is that updates may not appear everywhere instantly until you invalidate or the cache times out.

slides.headline: A CDN brings content closer to users; IaC makes the whole stack rebuildable from a file
slides.text: Production architecture is fast at the edge and reproducible at the core.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is System Design & Why It's Different From Coding

posts.title: What Is System Design & Why It's Different From Coding

slides.headline: You can write flawless code and still design a system that falls over at scale
slides.text: System design is a different discipline.

slides.headline: System design is deciding how components fit together to meet scale, reliability, and cost goals
slides.text: It's the architecture level: how data flows, where it's stored, how the pieces communicate, and how the whole thing behaves under load and failure.

slides.headline: Start from requirements and constraints, then choose components and trade-offs
slides.text: You clarify scale, latency, and consistency needs, estimate load, then pick storage, caching, and communication patterns that fit — justifying each choice.

slides.headline: Coding optimises a function; system design optimises the whole under real-world limits
slides.text: Good code makes one part correct; good design makes many parts cooperate reliably despite scale, failure, and money — often by choosing the least-bad trade-off.

slides.headline: Coding makes a component work; system design makes a hundred of them work together under load
slides.text: At scale, architecture decides success more than any single line.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal, Load Balancing & Caching

posts.title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal, Load Balancing & Caching

slides.headline: Your app is slow under load — do you buy a bigger server or add more servers?
slides.text: That fork is the heart of scaling.

slides.headline: Vertical scaling grows one machine; horizontal scaling adds more; load balancing and caching support both
slides.text: Scaling up means a bigger server; scaling out means many servers behind a load balancer; caching stores hot results so you compute them once.

slides.headline: Cache what's read often, spread requests across machines, add machines as needed
slides.text: Frequently-read data is served from cache; a load balancer distributes traffic; when demand grows, you add instances rather than a single ever-bigger box.

slides.headline: Vertical scaling is simple but capped; horizontal scales far but demands statelessness
slides.text: A bigger machine needs no code changes but hits a ceiling and a single point of failure; many machines scale nearly limitlessly but force you to handle shared state carefully.

slides.headline: Scale up hits a ceiling; scale out hits complexity — and a cache buys speed by risking staleness
slides.text: Every scaling move is a trade, not a free upgrade.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Database Replication & Sharding at Scale

posts.title: Database Replication & Sharding at Scale

slides.headline: One database served you fine — until reads overwhelmed it and it grew too big for one machine
slides.text: Replication and sharding split the load two ways.

slides.headline: Replication copies data across servers; sharding splits data across servers
slides.text: Replicas hold full copies to spread reads and survive failures; shards each hold a slice of the data to spread writes and storage.

slides.headline: Route reads to replicas, and route each record to the shard that owns it
slides.text: Read-heavy load fans out across replicas; each piece of data lives on one shard chosen by a key, so writes and storage divide across machines.

slides.headline: Replication scales reads but risks stale copies; sharding scales writes but complicates queries
slides.text: Replicas may lag the primary, so a read can be slightly out of date; shards spread write load but make queries that span shards, and rebalancing, genuinely hard.

slides.headline: Replication copies data to scale reads; sharding splits data to scale writes — each buys scale with a new headache
slides.text: Pick the split that matches whether reads or writes are drowning you.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Message Queues, Kafka & Event-Driven Architecture

posts.title: Message Queues, Kafka & Event-Driven Architecture

slides.headline: Your signup endpoint sent the welcome email inline — under a traffic spike, the whole request timed out
slides.text: A queue would have decoupled them.

slides.headline: A message queue lets services hand off work asynchronously; Kafka scales that to event streams
slides.text: A queue holds tasks so a producer can drop work and move on while a consumer processes it later; Kafka is a durable, high-throughput log of events many consumers can read.

slides.headline: Producers publish events, the broker buffers them, consumers process at their own pace
slides.text: Instead of doing slow work in the request, you publish an event; the broker stores it; workers consume and handle it independently, absorbing spikes.

slides.headline: Async decoupling adds resilience and scale but also eventual consistency and complexity
slides.text: Queues smooth spikes and isolate failures, so one slow service can't stall another; the cost is that work now completes later, and you must reason about ordering and retries.

slides.headline: A queue decouples 'accept the work' from 'do the work' — so a spike delays tasks instead of dropping requests
slides.text: Push slow work off the critical path and the system stops choking.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Microservices vs Monolith & the CAP Theorem

posts.title: Microservices vs Monolith & the CAP Theorem

slides.headline: 'Just use microservices' is advice that has sunk as many projects as it's saved
slides.text: The choice is a real trade-off, bounded by a theorem.

slides.headline: A monolith is one deployable unit; microservices split it into many; CAP bounds any distributed system
slides.text: A monolith keeps everything together; microservices break it into independently deployable services. CAP says under a network partition you can keep consistency or availability, not both.

slides.headline: Split by clear boundaries only when the coordination cost is worth it
slides.text: Microservices pay off when teams and domains are genuinely independent; before that, a monolith's single deploy and shared code are simpler and faster.

slides.headline: Microservices scale teams and parts independently but add network, ops, and consistency costs
slides.text: Independent services let teams move separately and scale hot paths alone; you pay with network calls, distributed failures, and the CAP trade you can't escape.

slides.headline: Microservices trade a coding problem for a distributed-systems problem — and CAP says you can't have it all
slides.text: Reach for them to solve organisational scale, not to feel modern.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Fault Tolerance, Distributed Systems, Rate Limiting & Idempotency

posts.title: Fault Tolerance, Distributed Systems, Rate Limiting & Idempotency

slides.headline: In a distributed system, failure isn't an edge case — it's Tuesday
slides.text: Fault tolerance and idempotency are how you survive it.

slides.headline: Fault tolerance keeps working through failures; idempotency makes retries safe; rate limiting protects capacity
slides.text: Redundancy and graceful degradation absorb failures; an idempotent operation gives the same result no matter how many times it runs; rate limits stop overload.

slides.headline: Assume things fail, retry safely, and cap load before it cascades
slides.text: Design so a dead node is handled, make operations safe to retry so a lost response can be resent without double-charging, and throttle before overload spreads.

slides.headline: Retries improve reliability but cause duplicates unless operations are idempotent
slides.text: Automatic retries recover from transient failures; without idempotency they can charge a card twice or send an email twice — retry safety is what makes retries usable.

slides.headline: In distributed systems things fail constantly — idempotency is what lets you retry without making it worse
slides.text: Build for failure as the default, not the exception.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing a URL Shortener From Scratch

posts.title: Designing a URL Shortener From Scratch

slides.headline: A URL shortener looks trivial until you ask: how do you guarantee every short code is unique at billions of scale?
slides.text: That's the whole design problem.

slides.headline: A URL shortener maps a short code to a long URL and redirects on lookup
slides.text: Generate a unique short key, store the mapping, and on each visit look up the key and issue a redirect to the original URL.

slides.headline: Create: generate a unique key, store it. Read: look up the key, redirect.
slides.text: Writes are rare and simple; reads are enormous and must be fast, so the lookup path is cached and the key generation avoids collisions.

slides.headline: This is a read-heavy system, so it's optimised with caching over write speed
slides.text: Far more people click short links than create them, so the design leans on caches and fast key-value lookups; write complexity (unique keys) is a one-time cost per link.

slides.headline: A URL shortener is a read-heavy key-value lookup — get unique keys and fast redirects right and the rest follows
slides.text: Design for the operation that happens a billion times, not the one that happens once.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing Instagram: A System Design Breakdown

posts.title: Designing Instagram: A System Design Breakdown

slides.headline: Instagram's real challenge isn't storing photos — it's building each user's feed fast, for hundreds of millions
slides.text: That's a fan-out problem.

slides.headline: The feed is the hard part: assembling recent posts from everyone you follow, instantly
slides.text: Storing and serving images is solved with object storage and a CDN; the design problem is generating personalised feeds at scale.

slides.headline: Pre-compute feeds by pushing posts to followers, or pull them on read
slides.text: Fan-out-on-write pushes a new post into every follower's feed cache for fast reads; fan-out-on-read assembles the feed when requested — most systems blend both.

slides.headline: Fan-out-on-write makes reads fast but explodes for celebrity accounts
slides.text: Pre-building feeds gives instant reads for normal users; a user with 50 million followers makes that write fan-out impossible, so popular accounts are handled with pull instead — a hybrid.

slides.headline: Instagram's scale problem is the feed, not the photos — and the fix is choosing where to pay the cost, on write or on read
slides.text: Design the timeline; storage is the easy part.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing WhatsApp: How Real-Time Messaging Scales

posts.title: Designing WhatsApp: How Real-Time Messaging Scales

slides.headline: WhatsApp's hard problem isn't sending a message — it's delivering it in real time when the recipient might be offline
slides.text: Presence and delivery at scale drive the design.

slides.headline: Real-time messaging needs persistent connections, message queues, and delivery guarantees
slides.text: Clients hold open connections so servers can push instantly; messages are queued when a recipient is offline and delivered on reconnect, with sent/delivered/read acknowledgements.

slides.headline: Sender to server, queue if offline, push on connect, acknowledge each step
slides.text: A message goes to the server, which either pushes it over the recipient's live connection or stores it until they reconnect, tracking each delivery state.

slides.headline: Persistent connections enable instant delivery but are expensive to hold at scale
slides.text: Keeping millions of always-open connections gives real-time push; it consumes server resources and demands careful connection management that plain request-response avoids.

slides.headline: Real-time chat is about connections and delivery state, not just moving text — offline delivery is the real design
slides.text: The message is easy; guaranteeing it arrives is the system.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing YouTube: Video at Massive Scale

posts.title: Designing YouTube: Video at Massive Scale

slides.headline: YouTube's problem isn't playing a video — it's serving petabytes to billions without the network melting
slides.text: Encoding and the CDN carry the weight.

slides.headline: Video at scale means transcoding into many formats and serving from the edge
slides.text: Each upload is transcoded into multiple resolutions and bitrates; a global CDN caches those chunks close to viewers so streams don't cross the world.

slides.headline: Upload, transcode into variants, distribute to edge, stream adaptively
slides.text: A video is processed into several quality levels, pushed to edge servers worldwide, and the player picks the bitrate that matches each viewer's connection.

slides.headline: Pre-transcoding and edge caching cost storage and processing but make global streaming smooth
slides.text: Generating many variants and caching them everywhere is expensive up front; it's what lets a video start instantly and adapt to any connection without buffering.

slides.headline: Streaming at scale is a transcoding-and-CDN problem — the play button is the easy 1%
slides.text: Move the bytes close to the viewer before they press play.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing Uber: Real-Time Location & Matching

posts.title: Designing Uber: Real-Time Location & Matching

slides.headline: Uber's core problem updates every few seconds: where is everyone, and who should get this ride?
slides.text: Real-time location and matching define it.

slides.headline: The system tracks live locations and matches riders to nearby drivers
slides.text: Drivers stream their position constantly; a geospatial index finds candidates near a rider; a matching service picks one and coordinates the trip.

slides.headline: Ingest locations, index them geographically, match on request, track the trip
slides.text: Continuous location updates feed a spatial index (like geohashing); a ride request queries nearby drivers; the match is made and both sides tracked in real time.

slides.headline: Real-time geospatial matching is powerful but write-heavy and latency-sensitive
slides.text: Constant location updates from millions of drivers are a firehose of writes; the payoff is fast, nearby matches — but the indexing and freshness are genuinely hard to keep cheap.

slides.headline: Uber is a real-time geospatial matching problem — the map is the database and freshness is everything
slides.text: Location that's seconds stale is a wrong match.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing Netflix: Streaming at Global Scale

posts.title: Designing Netflix: Streaming at Global Scale

slides.headline: Netflix's challenge is delivering flawless video to the whole planet at once, on any connection
slides.text: Its answer changed how the internet delivers content.

slides.headline: Global streaming relies on adaptive bitrate and caching content inside ISPs
slides.text: Video is chunked and offered at multiple qualities; Netflix places its own caching servers deep inside ISP networks so most streams never traverse the open internet.

slides.headline: Pre-position popular content near viewers, then stream the right quality per connection
slides.text: Popular titles are pushed to edge caches ahead of demand; the player continuously picks the bitrate that matches the viewer's bandwidth to avoid buffering.

slides.headline: Caching deep in the network gives quality and scale but requires massive pre-distribution
slides.text: Placing content inside ISPs makes streaming fast and offloads the backbone; it demands predicting what to cache where and shipping enormous amounts of data before anyone watches.

slides.headline: Netflix scales by moving content to the edge before you press play — prediction and caching, not raw bandwidth
slides.text: Serve from next door, not across the ocean.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Designing a Payment System: Handling Money Safely

posts.title: Designing a Payment System: Handling Money Safely

slides.headline: A payment system's bug isn't a glitch — it's someone's money charged twice or lost entirely
slides.text: Correctness outranks everything here.

slides.headline: Payment systems demand consistency, idempotency, and a full audit trail
slides.text: Money can't be double-spent or vanish, so operations must be atomic, retries must not double-charge, and every state change must be recorded.

slides.headline: Use idempotency keys, transactional writes, and immutable records of every step
slides.text: Each payment carries a unique key so retries are safe; balance changes commit as transactions; every action is logged immutably for reconciliation and disputes.

slides.headline: Prioritising correctness over speed is the right trade when money is involved
slides.text: Payment paths favour strong consistency and verification even at the cost of latency; a slower, provably-correct charge beats a fast one that might duplicate or lose funds.

slides.headline: A payment system trades speed for certainty — idempotency and audit trails matter more than milliseconds
slides.text: With money, being right beats being fast, always.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Python? (And the Fundamentals)

posts.title: Why Python? (And the Fundamentals)

slides.headline: For data and automation work, most teams reach for the same language first
slides.text: Python — and it's a deliberate choice, not just fashion.

slides.headline: Python is readable, batteries-included, and backed by a huge data ecosystem
slides.text: Its clean syntax lowers the barrier; its standard library and packages cover almost everything; and the data and ML world is built around it.

slides.headline: Write less code, lean on libraries, iterate fast
slides.text: Python's expressiveness and vast package ecosystem let you prototype and glue systems together quickly, which is why it dominates scripting and data work.

slides.headline: Python trades raw execution speed for developer speed and ecosystem
slides.text: It's slower than compiled languages at the CPU level; it wins by making humans faster and by wrapping fast C libraries — a great trade for data work, a poor one for tight loops.

slides.headline: Python optimises for the programmer, not the CPU — and for data work that's the right trade
slides.text: Fast to write beats fast to run when the bottleneck is you.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: OOP, Modules & File Handling in Python

posts.title: OOP, Modules & File Handling in Python

slides.headline: A script grows past a few hundred lines and turns into a tangle no one can follow
slides.text: OOP and modules are how Python stays organised.

slides.headline: OOP bundles data with behaviour; modules split code into files; file handling reads and writes data
slides.text: Classes group related state and methods; modules organise code across files with imports; file handling lets programs persist and load data from disk.

slides.headline: Model things as objects, separate concerns into modules, read and write files cleanly
slides.text: You represent entities as classes, keep related code in dedicated modules, and use context managers to open, use, and safely close files.

slides.headline: OOP organises complex state but can over-engineer simple scripts
slides.text: Classes shine when you have entities with shared behaviour and state; forced onto a small script they add ceremony without benefit — not everything needs to be an object.

slides.headline: OOP groups data with the code that acts on it; modules keep those groups from colliding
slides.text: Structure earns its keep as a program grows, not before.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Python for Automation: os, subprocess & APIs

posts.title: Python for Automation: os, subprocess & APIs

slides.headline: The most valuable Python you'll write may be the script that does your boring job while you sleep
slides.text: Automation is that leverage.

slides.headline: os and subprocess control the system; requests talks to APIs
slides.text: The os module manipulates files and the environment; subprocess runs other programs; the requests library calls web APIs to fetch and send data.

slides.headline: Script the manual task: touch files, run commands, call APIs, repeat on a schedule
slides.text: You replace repetitive clicks with a script that moves files, invokes tools, and pulls or pushes data via APIs — then schedule it to run itself.

slides.headline: Automation saves ongoing time but must handle failure it can't ask you about
slides.text: A script running unattended pays back forever; it also has to catch errors, retry, and log, because there's no human watching to react when something goes wrong.

slides.headline: Automation is writing the script once so the boring task runs itself forever after
slides.text: Trade an hour of scripting for a task you never do by hand again.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Pandas, NumPy & Matplotlib: Python for Data

posts.title: Pandas, NumPy & Matplotlib: Python for Data

slides.headline: Doing data analysis with raw Python loops is like digging a foundation with a spoon
slides.text: NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib are the power tools.

slides.headline: NumPy is fast arrays, Pandas is labelled tables, Matplotlib is plotting
slides.text: NumPy does vectorised math on arrays far faster than loops; Pandas gives you spreadsheet-like DataFrames; Matplotlib turns data into charts.

slides.headline: Load into a DataFrame, compute on arrays, visualise the result
slides.text: You read data into Pandas, clean and transform it, run vectorised NumPy operations under the hood, and plot findings with Matplotlib.

slides.headline: Vectorised operations are dramatically faster but use more memory and hide the loop
slides.text: Operating on whole arrays at once beats Python loops by orders of magnitude; it also loads data into memory at once and abstracts away the iteration you'd otherwise see.

slides.headline: NumPy computes, Pandas organises, Matplotlib shows — vectorised, not looped, is the whole trick
slides.text: Stop looping over data in Python; operate on it in bulk.

slides.text: Why Your App's Database Is Wrong for Analytics (OLTP vs OLAP)

posts.title: Why Your App's Database Is Wrong for Analytics (OLTP vs OLAP)

slides.headline: The database that runs your app is a terrible place to ask 'what were last year's trends?'
slides.text: OLTP and OLAP are built for opposite jobs.

slides.headline: OLTP handles many small live transactions; OLAP handles big analytical queries
slides.text: Transactional systems process orders, updates, and reads for the running app; analytical systems crunch huge volumes of historical data for reporting and insight.

slides.headline: Run the app on OLTP, then move data into OLAP for analysis
slides.text: Live operations hit the transactional store; that data is periodically copied and reshaped into an analytical store optimised for scanning and aggregation.

slides.headline: Row-oriented OLTP is fast for single records; column-oriented OLAP is fast for aggregates
slides.text: Storing rows together makes reading and writing one record quick; storing columns together makes summing millions of values quick — you can't optimise both in one store.

slides.headline: OLTP runs the business, OLAP understands it — same data, opposite designs
slides.text: Never make your transactional database do analytics; it's built for the other job.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Data Warehouses, Data Lakes & Big Data Pipelines

posts.title: Data Warehouses, Data Lakes & Big Data Pipelines

slides.headline: Your data is scattered across databases, files, and APIs — and analysts can't answer a single question across them
slides.text: Warehouses, lakes, and pipelines exist to fix that.

slides.headline: A warehouse stores structured data for analysis; a lake stores raw data of any type; pipelines move data between them
slides.text: A data warehouse holds cleaned, structured data ready to query; a data lake holds raw data as-is; pipelines extract, transform, and load data from sources into these stores.

slides.headline: Ingest from sources, transform, load into the warehouse or lake for analysis
slides.text: Pipelines pull from apps, files, and APIs on a schedule, reshape the data, and land it where analysts and ML can use it.

slides.headline: Warehouses are query-ready but rigid; lakes are flexible but can become swamps
slides.text: A warehouse enforces structure so queries are fast and reliable; a lake accepts anything cheaply but, without governance, turns into an unusable dump of files.

slides.headline: A warehouse is clean and structured, a lake is raw and flexible — pipelines are what feed both
slides.text: Central, queryable data is a system you build, not a place data lands by itself.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Data Cleaning & Visualization With Python

posts.title: Data Cleaning & Visualization With Python

slides.headline: Real-world data arrives messy — missing values, wrong types, duplicates — and models trust it blindly
slides.text: Cleaning is most of the job.

slides.headline: Data cleaning fixes messy data; visualization reveals what it's telling you
slides.text: Cleaning handles missing values, wrong types, and duplicates; visualization turns rows of numbers into patterns a human can actually see.

slides.headline: Inspect, clean, then plot to understand before you model
slides.text: You profile the data for problems, fix or drop bad rows, then chart distributions and relationships to form hypotheses before any modelling.

slides.headline: Time spent cleaning feels unglamorous but determines whether analysis means anything
slides.text: Cleaning is tedious and rarely demoed; skip it and every chart and model downstream is built on garbage — 'garbage in, garbage out' is not a cliché.

slides.headline: Clean before you conclude — dirty data produces confident, wrong answers
slides.text: Most of data science is preparation; the insight is the last mile.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Machine Learning? (AI vs ML vs Traditional Programming)

posts.title: Why Machine Learning? (AI vs ML vs Traditional Programming)

slides.headline: For years we told computers every rule; then some problems had too many rules to write
slides.text: Machine learning flips the approach.

slides.headline: Traditional programming codes the rules; ML learns the rules from examples
slides.text: Instead of writing 'if this, then that' for every case, you show the system many examples and it infers the pattern that maps input to output.

slides.headline: Feed labelled examples, let the model find the pattern, then predict on new data
slides.text: You provide inputs paired with correct answers; the model adjusts itself to fit them; then it generalises to inputs it hasn't seen.

slides.headline: ML handles problems too complex to hand-code but needs data and gives probabilistic answers
slides.text: It cracks tasks like image recognition no one can write rules for; the cost is hunger for quality data and outputs that are likely, not guaranteed, correct.

slides.headline: Traditional code is rules you write; machine learning is rules the data teaches the machine
slides.text: When the rules are too many to write, learn them from examples.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Datasets, Features, Labels & the Training Process

posts.title: Datasets, Features, Labels & the Training Process

slides.headline: 'The model was trained' hides the real question: trained on what, and toward what answer?
slides.text: Datasets, features, and labels are the answer.

slides.headline: A dataset holds examples; features are the inputs; labels are the correct outputs
slides.text: Each example is a row; its features are the measurable inputs the model reads; its label is the answer the model is trying to learn to produce.

slides.headline: Split the data, learn on the training set, tune, then test on unseen data
slides.text: You hold out data the model never sees during training; it learns patterns from the training set, and you measure real performance on the untouched test set.

slides.headline: More data usually helps, but only if it's representative and correctly labelled
slides.text: Volume improves learning up to a point; biased or mislabelled data teaches the wrong pattern, and no amount of it fixes that — quality gates quantity.

slides.headline: Features are what the model sees, labels are what it's aiming for — training is closing the gap between them
slides.text: A model is only as good as the examples you show it.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Supervised vs Unsupervised: Regression, Classification & Clustering

posts.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised: Regression, Classification & Clustering

slides.headline: Some ML learns from answers you give it; some finds structure with no answers at all
slides.text: That split defines the two main families.

slides.headline: Supervised learning trains on labelled data; unsupervised finds structure in unlabelled data
slides.text: With labels, the model learns to predict a known answer (regression for numbers, classification for categories); without labels, it groups similar items (clustering).

slides.headline: Have labels? Predict them. No labels? Discover groupings.
slides.text: Predicting a house price is regression; sorting emails into spam or not is classification; segmenting customers with no predefined groups is clustering.

slides.headline: Supervised is accurate but needs costly labels; unsupervised needs none but is harder to evaluate
slides.text: Labelled data enables precise prediction but is expensive to produce; unlabelled learning is cheap to start but its output has no ground truth to check against.

slides.headline: Supervised learning predicts known answers; unsupervised learning discovers unknown structure
slides.text: The presence of labels decides which kind of learning you can even do.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Overfitting, Underfitting & Feature Engineering

posts.title: Overfitting, Underfitting & Feature Engineering

slides.headline: A model scored 99% in training and failed in the real world — it memorised instead of learning
slides.text: That's overfitting.

slides.headline: Overfitting memorises the training data; underfitting is too simple to capture the pattern; feature engineering shapes better inputs
slides.text: Overfit models ace training and flop on new data; underfit models miss the pattern entirely; feature engineering crafts inputs that make the real pattern learnable.

slides.headline: Watch training vs validation performance to catch the imbalance
slides.text: If training accuracy climbs while validation accuracy falls, you're overfitting; if both stay poor, you're underfitting — the gap tells you which way to correct.

slides.headline: Fighting overfitting reduces variance but risks underfitting — it's a balance
slides.text: Simplifying the model or adding regularisation curbs memorisation; push too far and the model becomes too simple to learn anything — the bias-variance trade-off.

slides.headline: Overfitting memorises, underfitting oversimplifies — the goal is a model that generalises, not one that recites
slides.text: Test on data the model never saw, or you're measuring memory.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Evaluation Metrics: Precision, Recall, F1 & ROC-AUC

posts.title: Evaluation Metrics: Precision, Recall, F1 & ROC-AUC

slides.headline: A model that calls everything 'not cancer' can be 99% accurate and completely useless
slides.text: Accuracy alone lies.

slides.headline: Precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC measure what accuracy hides
slides.text: Precision is how many flagged positives were right; recall is how many real positives you caught; F1 balances them; ROC-AUC measures ranking across thresholds.

slides.headline: Choose the metric that matches the cost of each kind of error
slides.text: If false positives are costly, favour precision; if missing a positive is dangerous, favour recall; F1 when you need both; ROC-AUC to compare models overall.

slides.headline: Optimising precision usually lowers recall, and vice versa
slides.text: Being stricter to avoid false alarms means missing more true cases; being more inclusive to catch everything means more false alarms — you tune the trade to the stakes.

slides.headline: Accuracy hides failure on imbalanced data — precision and recall show who you missed and who you falsely flagged
slides.text: Pick the metric by which mistake actually hurts.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: From ML to Neural Networks & Deep Learning

posts.title: From ML to Neural Networks & Deep Learning

slides.headline: Classic ML plateaus on messy inputs like images and audio — you run out of features to hand-craft
slides.text: Neural networks learn the features themselves.

slides.headline: Neural networks learn their own features through layers, enabling deep learning
slides.text: Where classic ML needs you to engineer inputs, a neural network's layers automatically learn increasingly abstract representations from raw data.

slides.headline: Stack layers so each learns a higher-level feature from the last
slides.text: Early layers detect edges, later layers combine them into shapes and objects — the network builds its own feature hierarchy instead of you defining one.

slides.headline: Deep learning removes manual feature engineering but demands far more data and compute
slides.text: It cracks perception tasks classic ML can't and skips hand-crafting features; the price is huge datasets, heavy computation, and models that are hard to interpret.

slides.headline: Classic ML needs features you design; deep learning lets the network discover them from raw data
slides.text: When you can't hand-craft the features, let depth learn them.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Neural Networks Explained: Neurons, Weights & Bias

posts.title: Neural Networks Explained: Neurons, Weights & Bias

slides.headline: A neural network sounds mysterious until you see it's just numbers multiplied, added, and squished
slides.text: Neurons, weights, and biases are all there is.

slides.headline: A neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias, and applies an activation
slides.text: Each connection has a weight signalling importance; the bias shifts the result; the activation function decides whether and how strongly the neuron fires.

slides.headline: Inputs times weights, plus bias, through an activation — repeated across layers
slides.text: Every neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, offsets it, and passes it through a non-linear function; stacking these builds complex behaviour from simple parts.

slides.headline: Non-linear activations let networks learn complex patterns a linear model can't
slides.text: Without them, stacking layers just collapses to one linear step; adding non-linearity is what lets a network model curves, boundaries, and interactions.

slides.headline: A neuron is weights, a bias, and an activation — intelligence emerges from millions of them, not any one
slides.text: The magic is in the arrangement, not the neuron.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Forward Propagation, Loss & Backpropagation

posts.title: Forward Propagation, Loss & Backpropagation

slides.headline: A fresh network is random and useless — the whole trick is how it corrects itself
slides.text: Backpropagation is that mechanism.

slides.headline: Forward propagation makes a prediction, loss measures the error, backpropagation assigns blame
slides.text: Data flows forward to a prediction; the loss function scores how wrong it is; backprop computes how much each weight contributed to that error.

slides.headline: Predict, measure error, push the error backward, nudge every weight
slides.text: The network makes a guess, the loss quantifies the miss, gradients flow backward to each weight, and each is adjusted a little to reduce the error next time.

slides.headline: Bigger learning steps train faster but can overshoot and never settle
slides.text: A large learning rate moves quickly toward a solution and risks bouncing past it; a small one is stable but slow — tuning it is central to training well.

slides.headline: Forward makes the guess, loss measures the miss, backprop fixes the blame — learning is error, corrected millions of times
slides.text: A network learns by being wrong on purpose and adjusting.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Activation Functions: Why Networks Need Non-Linearity

posts.title: Activation Functions: Why Networks Need Non-Linearity

slides.headline: Stack a hundred layers with no activation function and you've built... one layer
slides.text: Without a non-linear step between them, the layers collapse back into a single linear operation.

slides.headline: An activation function decides whether and how strongly a neuron fires
slides.text: After the weighted sum, it applies a non-linear bend — ReLU, sigmoid, tanh — so the network can represent curves, not just straight lines.

slides.headline: Non-linearity is what lets stacked layers learn complex patterns
slides.text: Each layer's activation bends the space a little; stacked, those bends compose into decision boundaries a straight line could never draw.

slides.headline: ReLU is fast and gradient-friendly; sigmoid saturates and stalls learning
slides.text: ReLU passes positives and zeros out negatives — cheap and stable to train; sigmoid squashes everything into 0–1 but flattens at the ends, where gradients vanish and learning crawls.

slides.headline: Without a non-linear activation, a deep network is just an expensive straight line
slides.text: Non-linearity is the whole reason depth buys you anything.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Vanishing Gradients: Why Deep Networks Were Once Impossible to Train

posts.title: Vanishing Gradients: Why Deep Networks Were Once Impossible to Train

slides.headline: For years, adding more layers made networks worse — and no one could train them deep
slides.text: The signal that teaches the early layers faded to almost nothing on the way back.

slides.headline: In a deep network, gradients shrink as they travel backward
slides.text: Backprop multiplies many small numbers layer by layer; by the time the error reaches the first layers, it has all but vanished, so they barely learn.

slides.headline: ReLU, careful initialization, and residual connections revived deep learning
slides.text: Swapping saturating activations for ReLU, initializing weights with the right scale, and adding skip connections let the gradient reach the bottom layers intact.

slides.headline: Vanishing gradients freeze learning; exploding gradients blow it up
slides.text: Too-small gradients stall the early layers; too-large ones send weights to infinity — the same instability from opposite ends, tamed by the same fixes.

slides.headline: Deep learning didn't wait on a bigger idea — it waited on letting the gradient survive the trip back
slides.text: The breakthrough was plumbing, not genius.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Training vs Inference: Why AI Needs So Much Compute

posts.title: Training vs Inference: Why AI Needs So Much Compute

slides.headline: Training a model can cost millions in compute; running it costs a fraction of a cent
slides.text: They're two completely different workloads that people constantly confuse.

slides.headline: Training teaches the model; inference is the trained model answering
slides.text: Training adjusts billions of weights over huge data, again and again; inference runs the frozen weights forward once to produce an output.

slides.headline: GPUs win because both stages are massively parallel matrix math
slides.text: A GPU does thousands of the same multiply-add at once — exactly the operation neural networks are built from — which is why they, not CPUs, run AI.

slides.headline: Training is expensive and one-time; inference is cheap but runs forever
slides.text: You pay enormously to train once; then every user request is a cheap forward pass — but at scale those passes add up, which is why inference cost dominates in production.

slides.headline: Training is building the model; inference is using it — and at scale, using it is where the bill lives
slides.text: The pricey part is teaching; the recurring part is asking.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: CNNs, RNNs & the Rise of Transformers

posts.title: CNNs, RNNs & the Rise of Transformers

slides.headline: Different data shapes need different network shapes — images, sequences, and language each got their own
slides.text: CNNs, RNNs, then transformers.

slides.headline: CNNs handle grids like images, RNNs handle sequences, transformers handle both with attention
slides.text: CNNs exploit spatial locality for images; RNNs process sequences step by step for text and time series; transformers use attention to relate all positions at once.

slides.headline: CNNs scan for local patterns; RNNs carry memory; transformers weigh every token against every other
slides.text: A CNN slides filters over an image to detect features; an RNN passes a hidden state along a sequence; a transformer lets each element attend directly to all others in parallel.

slides.headline: Transformers parallelise and capture long-range context but are compute- and data-hungry
slides.text: RNNs process sequentially and forget distant context; transformers see everything at once and scale better, at the cost of far more computation and data.

slides.headline: CNNs see space, RNNs remember sequence, transformers attend to everything at once — architecture follows the data's shape
slides.text: The transformer won by relating every token to every other in parallel.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: What Is Generative AI & What Is an LLM?

posts.title: What Is Generative AI & What Is an LLM?

slides.headline: Predictive AI labels what exists; generative AI produces what didn't — that's a genuine shift
slides.text: And an LLM is the engine behind the text kind.

slides.headline: Generative AI creates new content; an LLM is a model trained to predict the next token
slides.text: Instead of classifying inputs, generative models produce new text, images, or audio; a large language model does this for text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next piece.

slides.headline: Predict the next token, append it, repeat — coherent text emerges
slides.text: Given the text so far, the model outputs a probability over possible next tokens, picks one, adds it, and repeats — fluent output from a loop of predictions.

slides.headline: LLMs generate fluent, flexible text but can state falsehoods confidently
slides.text: Next-token prediction produces remarkably capable, general text; the same mechanism has no built-in grasp of truth, so it can be fluently, confidently wrong.

slides.headline: An LLM doesn't retrieve answers — it predicts the next token, one at a time, until it has a response
slides.text: Fluency is prediction, not knowledge — which is why it can be sure and wrong.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Tokens & Context Windows: How LLMs Actually Read Text

posts.title: Tokens & Context Windows: How LLMs Actually Read Text

slides.headline: An LLM never sees your words — it sees numbered chunks, and it can only hold so many at once
slides.text: Those chunks are tokens, and the ceiling on how many fit is the context window.

slides.headline: A token is a piece of text; the context window is how many fit at once
slides.text: Text is split into tokens — roughly word-pieces — each mapped to a number; the model can only attend to a fixed number of them per request.

slides.headline: Your prompt, the retrieved docs, and the reply all compete for one window
slides.text: Prompt, conversation history, retrieved context, and the answer share a single token budget; overflow it and the earliest content falls out of view.

slides.headline: A bigger context window sees more but costs more and can lose focus
slides.text: More tokens let the model consider more at once; they also cost more per call and can dilute attention across a huge window — bigger isn't free, or always better.

slides.headline: An LLM reads in tokens and thinks inside a fixed window — everything you send competes for that space
slides.text: The context window is the model's entire field of view.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers Demystified

posts.title: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers Demystified

slides.headline: How does a model that only does math understand that 'king' and 'queen' are related?
slides.text: Embeddings and attention are the answer.

slides.headline: Embeddings turn words into vectors of meaning; attention lets tokens weigh each other; transformers combine both
slides.text: An embedding places each token in a space where similar meanings sit close; attention lets each token decide which others matter for it; the transformer stacks this into understanding.

slides.headline: Embed tokens into vectors, then let attention mix in the relevant context
slides.text: Words become numeric vectors capturing meaning; attention updates each token's representation using the tokens it deems relevant, so 'bank' near 'river' differs from 'bank' near 'money'.

slides.headline: Attention captures context brilliantly but its cost grows with the square of sequence length
slides.text: Relating every token to every other gives rich context understanding; that all-pairs comparison makes long inputs expensive — the core scaling challenge of transformers.

slides.headline: Embeddings give tokens meaning, attention gives them context — together they let math 'understand' language
slides.text: Meaning is a position in space; context is what attention pulls in.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Temperature & Sampling: Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers

posts.title: Temperature & Sampling: Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers

slides.headline: You sent the identical prompt twice and got two different answers — that's not a bug
slides.text: It's the sampling settings deciding how much randomness to allow.

slides.headline: The model outputs probabilities; sampling picks which token to actually use
slides.text: At each step it ranks every possible next token; temperature and top-p control how far it's willing to stray from the single most likely one.

slides.headline: Low temperature is focused and repeatable; high temperature is varied and creative
slides.text: Near zero it almost always picks the top token — consistent, sometimes bland; higher, it samples further down the list — more variety, more risk of nonsense.

slides.headline: Deterministic output is reliable but rigid; sampled output is creative but inconsistent
slides.text: Set it low for facts, code, and anything you need repeatable; set it higher for brainstorming and copy — the right setting depends on whether you want the same answer twice.

slides.headline: Temperature is the model's boldness dial — low for correct, high for creative
slides.text: Same prompt, different answers is a setting, not a fault.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Prompting, System Prompts & Structured Outputs

posts.title: Prompting, System Prompts & Structured Outputs

slides.headline: The same model gives a mediocre or an excellent answer depending only on how you asked
slides.text: Prompting is a real skill, not a trick.

slides.headline: The prompt is your instruction; the system prompt sets behaviour; structured outputs force a usable format
slides.text: What you type steers the model; a system prompt shapes its role and rules across the whole session; asking for JSON or a schema makes output a program can parse.

slides.headline: Set the role, give clear instructions and examples, and specify the output shape
slides.text: You establish context and constraints in a system prompt, state the task precisely with examples, and request a defined format so the response is predictable and machine-readable.

slides.headline: Clear, constrained prompts improve reliability but can reduce creative range
slides.text: Tight instructions and formats make outputs consistent and parseable; over-constraining can box the model out of better, more flexible answers — match the leash to the task.

slides.headline: The model's quality is bounded by your prompt — vague in, vague out; precise in, usable out
slides.text: How you ask is part of the system, not a footnote.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why LLMs Hallucinate (And What Actually Reduces It)

posts.title: Why LLMs Hallucinate (And What Actually Reduces It)

slides.headline: An LLM cited a court case that never existed — confidently, in perfect legal formatting
slides.text: It wasn't lying; it was doing exactly what it's built to do.

slides.headline: A hallucination is fluent text that isn't true — a side effect of next-token prediction
slides.text: The model optimizes for plausible continuations, not verified facts; when it doesn't know, it still produces the most likely-sounding answer.

slides.headline: Grounding the model in real sources is what reduces it
slides.text: Retrieval feeds it actual documents to answer from, and asking for citations or 'I don't know' lowers confident invention — you constrain it toward evidence.

slides.headline: Fluency and factuality are different targets, and the base model optimizes for the first
slides.text: The same mechanism that makes output sound expert makes it sound expert when it's wrong — cutting hallucination means adding truth constraints the model doesn't have on its own.

slides.headline: An LLM predicts what sounds right, not what is right — grounding it in sources is how you close the gap
slides.text: Confidence is not evidence; fluency is not fact.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Fine-Tuning, RAG & Vector Databases

posts.title: Fine-Tuning, RAG & Vector Databases

slides.headline: An LLM knows nothing about your private documents and can't learn today's news on its own
slides.text: Fine-tuning and RAG solve two different halves of that.

slides.headline: Fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights; RAG retrieves facts at query time from a vector database
slides.text: Fine-tuning teaches new behaviour or style by training on examples; RAG leaves the model unchanged and instead fetches relevant documents to include in the prompt.

slides.headline: Embed your documents, retrieve the relevant ones, and feed them to the model with the question
slides.text: Your data is turned into vectors and stored; at query time the most relevant chunks are retrieved and added to the prompt so the model answers from real, current sources.

slides.headline: Fine-tuning changes behaviour but is costly and static; RAG adds fresh knowledge but depends on retrieval quality
slides.text: Fine-tuning bakes in style and skills yet must be redone as data changes; RAG updates instantly by swapping documents but only helps if it retrieves the right ones.

slides.headline: Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves; RAG changes what it knows right now — different problems, different tools
slides.text: Teach behaviour by tuning; supply knowledge by retrieving.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Why Chatbots Aren't Agents (And What Actually Makes an Agent)

posts.title: Why Chatbots Aren't Agents (And What Actually Makes an Agent)

slides.headline: A chatbot answers and stops; you asked it to 'book the trip' and it just... described how to
slides.text: The gap between those is what makes an agent.

slides.headline: An agent doesn't just respond — it takes actions in a loop to achieve a goal
slides.text: A chatbot maps input to output once; an agent plans, uses tools, observes results, and keeps going until the goal is met or it gives up.

slides.headline: Reason about the goal, act with a tool, observe, then decide the next step
slides.text: Given an objective, the agent chooses an action, executes it (search, API call, code), reads the outcome, and loops — using each result to inform the next move.

slides.headline: Agents accomplish multi-step goals but add unpredictability and failure modes chatbots don't have
slides.text: Autonomy lets them actually do things across steps; it also means they can loop, take wrong actions, or compound errors — capability and risk rise together.

slides.headline: A chatbot responds; an agent acts, observes, and decides again — the loop is what makes it an agent
slides.text: The difference isn't smarter answers, it's taking steps toward a goal.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Tool Calling, Memory & Planning: How Agents Think

posts.title: Tool Calling, Memory & Planning: How Agents Think

slides.headline: A model alone can't check the weather, remember yesterday, or break a big task into steps
slides.text: Tools, memory, and planning are the scaffolding that give it those abilities.

slides.headline: Tool calling lets an agent act, memory lets it retain context, planning lets it sequence steps
slides.text: Tools connect the model to the real world (search, APIs, code); memory persists information across turns and sessions; planning decomposes a goal into ordered sub-tasks.

slides.headline: Plan the steps, call tools to execute them, store results in memory for later steps
slides.text: The agent breaks a goal into sub-tasks, invokes the right tool for each, and writes outcomes to memory so later steps can build on earlier ones.

slides.headline: More tools and memory expand capability but widen the attack and error surface
slides.text: Each tool an agent can call and each thing it remembers makes it more capable and gives more ways to be misused, poisoned, or to go wrong — power and risk scale together.

slides.headline: Tools let an agent act, memory lets it remember, planning lets it sequence — capability comes from the model plus its scaffolding
slides.text: The intelligence is the model; the usefulness is the scaffolding around it.

slides.headline: Coming next
slides.text: Agent Loops, Multi-Step Tasks & Real-World Agents

posts.title: Agent Loops, Multi-Step Tasks & Real-World Agents

slides.headline: Real tasks aren't one step — 'research this and write a summary' is a dozen actions in sequence
slides.text: The agent loop is what strings them together.

slides.headline: The agent loop repeats reason-act-observe until a multi-step task is done
slides.text: Each cycle the agent decides the next action, executes it, and evaluates the result, continuing until the goal is reached or a stopping condition triggers.

slides.headline: Loop: decide, act, observe, check if done — repeat or stop
slides.text: The agent assesses progress, takes the next action, reads the outcome, and either continues the loop or ends — with limits to prevent it running forever.

slides.headline: Longer loops handle harder tasks but risk drift, cost, and runaway execution
slides.text: More iterations let agents tackle complex goals; they also accumulate cost, can wander off-task, and need guardrails and step limits so a stuck agent doesn't loop endlessly.

slides.headline: An agent handles multi-step work by looping reason-act-observe until it's done — with a leash so it stops
slides.text: Real-world tasks are loops, not single replies.

posts.title: AI Workflows, Multi-Agent Systems & MCP

slides.headline: One agent doing everything gets confused; a fixed script can't adapt — the middle ground is structure
slides.text: Workflows, multi-agent systems, and MCP provide it.

slides.headline: Workflows are predefined paths; multi-agent systems split work across specialised agents; MCP standardises tool access
slides.text: A workflow fixes the steps for reliability; multiple agents each own a role and coordinate; the Model Context Protocol gives models a standard way to connect to tools and data.

slides.headline: Use fixed workflows where reliability matters, agents where flexibility does, MCP to connect both to tools
slides.text: Predictable tasks run as workflows; open-ended ones use agents; MCP provides a common interface so any of them can reach external systems the same way.

slides.headline: Workflows are predictable but rigid; multi-agent systems are flexible but harder to control
slides.text: Fixed paths give reliability and are easy to reason about; autonomous agents adapt to the unexpected but coordinate unpredictably — most real systems blend the two.

slides.headline: Workflows give reliability, agents give flexibility, MCP gives them a common way to reach the world
slides.text: Choose structure where you need certainty and autonomy where you need adaptability.

posts.title: Evaluating & Securing Production AI Agents

slides.headline: An agent that can act can also act wrongly — or be tricked into it — at machine speed
slides.text: Evaluation and security aren't optional for production agents.

slides.headline: Evaluation measures whether the agent actually works; security defends against misuse like prompt injection
slides.text: Evals test task success, cost, and failure rates systematically; security guards against manipulated inputs, tool misuse, and leaking data the agent shouldn't touch.

slides.headline: Test on real tasks, constrain tool permissions, and watch for injected instructions
slides.text: You benchmark the agent on representative tasks, limit each tool to least privilege, and validate inputs so hidden instructions in fetched content can't hijack it.

slides.headline: Broad autonomy is powerful but every capability is also a new attack vector
slides.text: The more an agent can do, the more useful and the more dangerous when compromised; locking it down reduces risk and also the very autonomy that made it valuable.

slides.headline: A production agent must be measured and constrained — capability without evaluation and guardrails is a liability
slides.text: Powerful and unchecked is not deployable; test it and fence it.

posts.title: Building Your First AI Agent (Then a Multi-Agent System)

slides.headline: The gap from 'I understand agents' to 'I built one' is smaller than it looks — and one agent leads to many
slides.text: Here's the shape of building it.

slides.headline: A first agent is a model, a set of tools, and a loop; a multi-agent system coordinates several
slides.text: Give a model access to tools and wrap it in a reason-act-observe loop and you have an agent; give each of several agents a role and a way to hand off, and you have a system.

slides.headline: Start with one agent and a few tools, then split roles as the task grows
slides.text: Build a single agent that plans and calls tools; when the task spans distinct skills, break it into specialised agents that pass work between them.

slides.headline: Multi-agent systems handle bigger problems but add coordination and failure complexity
slides.text: Splitting work across agents scales to harder tasks and cleaner responsibilities; it also introduces communication overhead and new ways for the system to deadlock or misfire.

slides.headline: An agent is a model, tools, and a loop; a multi-agent system is several of those learning to hand off
slides.text: Start with one agent that works, then divide the labour.
